issues.body:
Context: verified on a live setup — OpenClaw gateway 2026.11.3 (Linux) with a paired, approved Pixel 10 Pro running the Android node app 2026.11.6-debug-dev (Accessibility Control enabled). This is a feature proposal with a concrete surface and acceptance criteria.



[Android Node] Add `device.apps.launch` — let an approved agent open apps on a paired phone

## Environment observed

- Gateway: OpenClaw 2026.11.3 (`847611d`), Linux host
- Android node app: `2026.11.6-debug-dev` on Pixel 10 Pro, connected + approved, Accessibility Control enabled (mobileUI live)
- Verified 2026-11-23 via `openclaw nodes describe`: declared Android command set is
  `camera.list, location.get, notifications.list, notifications.actions, system.notify, device.info, device.status, device.permissions, device.health, device.apps, contacts.search, calendar.events, callLog.search, motion.activity, motion.pedometer, mobile.ui.observe, mobile.ui.act, talk.ptt.*` — **no launch/open/intent command**
- Docs cross-check: `docs/nodes/device-commands.md` documents `device.apps` as listing-only; `docs/nodes/command-policy.md` Android row matches the read-only set above.

## Problem

`mobile.ui.act` can only drive the app that is already foregrounded. The moment a task
needs a *different* app ("open Tasker and build this task," "open Chrome and check X"),
the agent stalls and the owner has to unlock + open the app manually before the agent
can continue. That breaks the core promise of phone-driving for any multi-app flow,
which is exactly where agents help most.

Current workarounds are poor:

- Notification-listener sentinel + third-party automation app (Tasker/MacroDroid) event
  → launch app. Works, but is per-app setup, third-party dependent, and fragile.
- Owner opens the app first, then says "go." Adds a human round-trip to every flow.

## Proposal

Add one command to the `device.apps` family:

```
device.apps.launch
params: {
  "packageName": "net.dinglisch.android.taskerm",  // required; from device.apps listing
  "reason": "Building GM Board widget"             // optional; shown to the owner in a heads-up notification
}
result: {
  "launched": true,
  "packageName": "net.dinglisch.android.taskerm",
  "activity": "net.dinglisch.android.taskerm/.Activities.Tasker"
}
errors: APP_NOT_FOUND | APP_NOT_LAUNCHABLE (disabled/no launcher intent) | DEVICE_LOCKED | SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
```

Optional stretch (follow-up, not blocking): `deepLink` support for URL-scheme launches.

**Explicit non-goals:** launching from the lock screen (hard refusal), killing apps,
placing widgets, or driving the launcher itself — home-grid gestures stay owner-only,
consistent with the existing human-domain rule.

## Security & permission model (mirrors existing patterns)

1. **App-side toggle** in OpenClaw Android settings: "Allow app launching" — default
   OFF, same pattern as Installed Apps sharing for `device.apps`.
2. **Declaration + pairing approval:** the command is declared only while the toggle is
   on; per `command-policy.md`, a widened declaration triggers the existing
   `openclaw nodes pending` → `openclaw nodes approve <requestId>` flow on reconnect.
   One-time, persistent, revocable by turning the toggle off.
3. **Gateway ceiling:** add `device.apps.launch` to the Android default row in
   `command-policy.md`. Operators who don't want it block it with
   `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` (which always wins).
   - Rationale for keeping it out of the "dangerous persistent opt-in" list: launching
     itself surfaces no data — all visibility remains gated by Accessibility Control —
     and it is the agent equivalent of the owner tapping an icon. If maintainers prefer
     the stricter reading (silent foregrounding of sensitive apps like banking), an
     acceptable alternative is classifying it under `gateway.nodes.commands.allow`.
     Either model is fine; pick one and document it.
4. **UX guardrail:** when `reason` is provided, always surface it as a brief
   heads-up/bubble at launch, so an app opening is never unexplained to the owner.

## Implementation sketch (Android)

- `PackageManager.getLaunchIntentForPackage(pkg)` + `FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK`, started
  from the existing foreground node service (the same process that fulfills
  talk/notifications actions).
- Package visibility: reuse whatever `device.apps` listing already does (the app can
  already enumerate visible packages); avoid adding `QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES` if listing
  doesn't use it.
- Locked-device check (`KeyguardManager.isKeyguardLocked`) → return `DEVICE_LOCKED`
  instead of attempting, consistent with the lock-screen-is-owner-only rule.
- Structured errors, never silent failures — consistent with the other `device.*`
  commands.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `openclaw nodes invoke --node <id> --command device.apps.launch --params '{"packageName":"net.dinglisch.android.taskerm","reason":"Agent request"}'` opens the app on an unlocked device; returns `DEVICE_LOCKED` when locked.
- [ ] With the app toggle OFF, the command is undeclared; turning it ON triggers the pending → approve flow on reconnect.
- [ ] `gateway.nodes.commands.deny: ["device.apps.launch"]` blocks it end-to-end.
- [ ] Docs updated: `command-policy.md` Android row and `device-commands.md` family entry; agent-facing tool schema exposed via `nodes invoke` (and later, optionally, a `launch` affordance inside the mobile_ui act schema).

## Why this unlocks real value

End-to-end mobile loops become possible with zero third-party glue:
agent opens the app → `mobile.ui.act` drives it → owner does only what's genuinely
human (unlock, biometrics, launcher drags). The current 2-of-3 coverage is what forces
workarounds today.

## Related

- `docs/nodes/mobile-ui-driving` workflows (agent-side): today limited to in-app driving
- iOS equivalent would need a different mechanism (URL schemes); out of scope here.

issues.body:
## Problem

Release-path state upgrades copy only the state directory into the private shadow. An agent database registered at an absolute path outside the state directory (for example a custom `session.store` or agent location) is not copied, and the shadow Doctor can write to it directly:

- `src/state/openclaw-agent-db-registry.ts:99-103` registers it; `src/state/openclaw-state-db.paths.ts:74-93` keeps the absolute path when it is outside the state root.
- The SQLite shadow rewrite (`rewriteSqlitePrefix`) replaces only the state directory prefix, so the path stays unchanged.
- Doctor writers that follow registry entries: `doctor-agent-memory-schema.ts:137-140` (migrates the database at `entry.path`), `doctor-usage-cost-cache.ts:213-224` (retires the cost cache at `entry.path`).

If the candidate then fails its trial, the launcher restores the state directory originals but not these external files. The previous release may then meet an agent database that was already migrated.

Affects SQLite today and PostgreSQL state (#204363) equally. Found from source while designing #204363; not reproduced end to end yet.

## Expected

A failed update leaves every database the previous release reads in a state that release can use, including agent databases outside the state directory.

issues.body:
### Summary

On 2026.11.6, the session observer disables itself ("returned invalid JSON twice") when the
utility model is `anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5` (via claude-cli). The rejected outputs are
syntactically valid JSON: the model copies a `revision` field from the `previousDigest` in
the user payload into its answer, and `ModelDigestSchema` is a `strictObject`, so the extra
key rejects the whole digest.

Same family as #175646 (`planProgress: null` leaking from the payload), but a different
leaked field that nobody has reported yet.

### Root cause (source inspection, 2026.11.6 dist)

- `buildSessionObserverPrompt` strips only `sessionId` and `lifecycleRevision` from
  `previousDigest`; `revision` (and other internal fields) are sent to the model.
- The system prompt's example contains only headline/assessment/health/planProgress, but
  small models mimic the shape of `previousDigest`.
- `normalizeSessionObserverModelOutput` -> `safeParseJsonWithSchema(ModelDigestSchema)`
  with `strictObject` -> unknown key `revision` -> null -> retry -> null -> run disabled.
- The logged "last rejected output" is capped at 160 chars, so the extra key is never
  visible in the log (it appears after `assessment`).

### Reproduction

`SESSION_OBSERVER_SYSTEM_PROMPT` verbatim, a user payload shaped like
`buildSessionObserverPrompt` output (previousDigest with `revision`, 4 notes,
`planProgress: null`), validated with the shipped `normalizeSessionObserverModelOutput`.
6 calls per model:

| Model | Pass | Rejected keys |
|---|---|---|
| claude-haiku-5-5 | 4/6 | `headline,assessment,health,revision` (x2) |
| claude-sonnet-5-5 | 6/6 | - |

Real log line:

```
session observer disabled after consecutive failures
{consecutiveFailures: 2, error: "session observer returned invalid JSON twice; last rejected output: {\"headline\":\"Wrapping up workspace onboarding\",\"assessment\":\"The main agent finished ..."}
```

### Related

- `utilityModel.fallbacks` does not help on this build: fallback triggers only on call
  errors, and an invalid-but-successful Haiku answer is accepted by the chain before the
  observer rejects it (#196345 addresses this; not observed in 2026.11.6 behavior).

### Suggested fixes (any one would resolve it)

1. Send only model-facing fields in `previousDigest` (headline, assessment, health,
   planProgress), dropping `revision`, `runId`, `updatedAt`, etc.
2. Strip unknown keys (`.strip()` / pick known fields) instead of rejecting the digest.
3. Log the full rejected key set (not just a 160-char prefix) so this is diagnosable.

### Environment

OpenClaw 2026.11.6 (app-managed), macOS 27.2.1 arm64, utility model
anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5 via claude-cli runtime, no utility fallbacks.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

DeepSeek usage loses usable balances when `balance_infos` also contains a null row or a row with a numeric currency and a valid amount.

### Steps to reproduce

This is a synthetic malformed-response reproduction, not a report of a live DeepSeek incident.

1. Use OpenClaw source at `c99807a541c86cc49ffcc4d9dbabd1219f65bc53`.
2. Call `fetchDeepSeekUsage` from `src/plugin-sdk/provider-usage.ts` with a synthetic JSON response containing the following valid row and either malformed row. Try the malformed row both before and after the valid row.

   ```js
   const valid = {
     currency: " usd ", total_balance: "1.25",
     granted_balance: "0.25", topped_up_balance: "1"
   };
   const malformedRows = [null, { currency: 42, total_balance: "9" }];
   // Payload for each malformed row:
   // { is_available: true, balance_infos: [malformed, valid] }
   // { is_available: true, balance_infos: [valid, malformed] }
   ```

   The supported `fetchFn` argument can supply this response without provider credentials:

   ```js
   await fetchDeepSeekUsage("synthetic-key", 5000, async () =>
     new Response(JSON.stringify(payload), {
       status: 200, headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }
     })
   );
   ```

3. Compare with `balance_infos: [valid]`, which returns the expected balance summary and USD billing entry.

### Expected behavior

Keep the usable sibling balance, as in the valid-only control: `Balance $1.25 · Granted $0.25 · Topped up $1.00`, with a balance billing entry of `1.25 USD`. Malformed rows should not discard the entire provider result. Rows with a present non-string currency should be skipped; existing missing/null currency behavior should remain intact.

### Actual behavior

Both row orders reject instead of returning the valid balance:

```text
null-before: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'total_balance')
null-after: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'total_balance')
numeric-currency-before: TypeError: currency?.trim is not a function
numeric-currency-after: TypeError: currency?.trim is not a function
```

The usage loader catches the exception per provider, so the DeepSeek result becomes an error snapshot without its usable balance. This does not crash the Gateway or discard all providers.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.3 source at `c99807a541c86cc49ffcc4d9dbabd1219f65bc53`

### Operating system

macOS 27.0.1, arm64; Node v26.12.1

### Install method

Source checkout with pnpm dependencies; repository test runner and source SDK entry point.

### Model

No inference model is invoked; this exercises the DeepSeek account-balance usage fetch.

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw provider-usage SDK → DeepSeek balance fetcher → synthetic HTTP response. Runtime validation used a loopback HTTP server through the existing `fetchFn` argument, with the production URL asserted and only transport redirected locally.

### Logs

The real HTTP reproduction made five requests: the valid-only control passed, and all four malformed sibling cases failed with the errors above. The server verified GET `/user/balance`, the synthetic Bearer header, and `Accept: application/json`. All owned connections and the listener were closed afterward.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The existing owner suite passes on the unmodified source. Added owner regressions fail at the null dereference and currency trim on that source, then pass with row validation. With the correction, the identical HTTP proof returns the valid-only summary and billing for all five cases:

```text
valid-only: PASS
null-before: PASS
null-after: PASS
numeric-currency-before: PASS
numeric-currency-after: PASS
HTTP requests: 5; contract failures: 0
HTTP listener and connections closed
```

### Impact and severity

Affected surface: DeepSeek provider usage/balance reporting. A malformed sibling row hides usable balance information for that provider. The four synthetic malformed cases fail deterministically on the tested source. Production occurrence and frequency: NOT_ENOUGH_INFO.

### Additional information

The fetcher validates the top-level object and balance array, but asserts the row types before dereferencing `total_balance` and calling `currency?.trim()`. The top-level protection from #110785 does not validate individual rows. The single-pass aggregation from #148925 can be retained while validating rows at this boundary.

Fix: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/199644

## Symptom

In the browser Control UI's split Talk (STT/TTS) mode, a reply can stay silent and microphone capture does not resume, even when the Gateway returns synthesized audio.

## Reproduction and evidence

On a development build in headless Chromium with default audio output, start split Talk and let it receive a reply. The silent unlock clip's play promise did not settle in the trace:

```text
03:45:14.801Z play() data
03:45:15.019Z loadedmetadata prime 0 0.000045
03:45:18.403Z stalled prime 0 0.000045
```

The deterministic reproduction on upstream `22a57c95b6c` replaces the silent clip's `play()` with a pending promise, then supplies a successful `talk.speak` response. Expected: the reply starts and Talk can resume capture after it ends. Actual: only the silent clip calls `play()`.

In `ui/src/lib/speech-playback.ts`, `GatewaySpeechPlayback.prepare()` saves the primer's play promise. `speak()` waits for that promise or cancellation, with no deadline.

issues.body:
### Summary

Channel pairing can list pending requests, approve one and dismiss one. There is no way, over the Gateway protocol or the CLI, to see who has already been approved or to take an approval back. An approval made by mistake stays until someone edits the store by hand.

### Problem to solve

Read on `main` (a0aecac243c, 2026-11-11) and on `v2026.11.3`:

- Gateway methods: `channels.pairing.list`, `channels.pairing.approve`, `channels.pairing.dismiss` (`src/gateway/methods/core-descriptors.ts`). `list` returns pending requests only.
- CLI: `openclaw pairing list` ("List pending pairing requests") and `openclaw pairing approve` (`src/cli/pairing-cli.ts`).
- The store already has both halves internally: `readChannelAllowFromStoreSync` and `removeChannelAllowFromStoreEntry` (`src/pairing/pairing-store.ts`). Nothing exposes them.

For an operator UI built on the Gateway protocol (a dashboard that shows the pairing inbox and lets the operator approve), this leaves two gaps:

1. The operator cannot answer "who can message this agent right now?" for a channel in pairing mode. Config `allowFrom` is visible; store approvals are not.
2. The operator cannot remove one approved sender. The only way to drop an approval is to switch the channel to a strict allowlist, or to edit the store out of band.

#56621 asked for the CLI side of this and was closed by the stale bot on 2026-08-23 without a decision; this request is for the Gateway methods, with the CLI as a thin wrapper.

### Proposed solution

Two methods next to the existing three, same scope (`operator.pairing`):

- `channels.pairing.listApproved { channel, accountId? }` → `{ entries: [{ id, approvedAt?, name? }] }`, read from the pairing allow-from store for that channel account.
- `channels.pairing.revoke { channel, accountId?, id }` → `{ removed: boolean }`, calling `removeChannelAllowFromStoreEntry`. It should take effect for the next inbound message without a restart, as an approval does.

And the matching CLI: `openclaw pairing list --approved` and `openclaw pairing revoke <channel> <id>`.

### Alternatives considered

- Switching the channel to `dmPolicy: "allowlist"`: drops the store for everyone, not for one sender, and changes the access mode.
- Reading or editing the store directly: not available to a remote operator client, and it bypasses the Gateway.

### Impact

Every deployment that uses pairing with more than one approved sender, and every operator UI on top of the Gateway. It is an access-control question operators ask early: "who did I let in, and how do I take that back?"

### Evidence/examples

- `src/gateway/methods/core-descriptors.ts`: the three `channels.pairing.*` descriptors.
- `src/pairing/pairing-store.ts`: `readChannelAllowFromStoreSync`, `addChannelAllowFromStoreEntry`, `removeChannelAllowFromStoreEntry`.
- #56621 (closed as stale).

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Not at the moment. Happy to test a build and report back.

issues.body:
## Observed behavior

OpenClaw 2026.9.6 on macOS with Node 24.19.0 logged a successful agent database opening that took 128.846 seconds. Its synchronous integrity and foreign-key checks accounted for 128.816 seconds. The outcome was healthy, canonical index validation took 14 milliseconds, and no indexes were repaired. An earlier measurement put the database file at approximately 2.96 GB.

The delay nearly filled the interval before model transport began, but the database row lacked a request trace. We cannot prove that it caused the whole subsequent request timeout, or identify the worker entrypoint and receipt/proof state at that opening.

## Relevant upstream change

[The merged peer-worker integrity reuse fix](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/155785) addresses repeated checks with peer leases and an absent persisted verification receipt. The relevant receipt-dependent conditions remain in the published version's [reuse predicate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.9.6/src/state/openclaw-quarantine-store.ts#L116), [schema admission](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.9.6/src/state/openclaw-agent-db-schema.ts#L150), and [receipt publication](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.9.6/src/state/openclaw-agent-db-lease.ts#L311), matching our installed code.

This is a plausible candidate, not a confirmed reproduction of that bug. We have not run the upstream synthetic regression on this host. The package channel lookup on September 29 still returned 2026.9.6 for latest and beta.

Could you identify a supported release or backport containing this change, or the minimum additional diagnostics needed to distinguish this case? We want to preserve the existing integrity and migration safeguards.

## Investigation boundary

A temporary logging-only patch was installed for one passive 15-minute observation. No diagnostic marker appeared. All five original module files were restored and verified; already-loaded logging code could remain until the corresponding worker naturally exits. No additional database check, forced worker start, restart, or repair was performed during that observation.

This report contains no database contents, credentials, local filesystem paths, account identifiers, or case research. No attachments are proposed.

issues.body:
## Summary

`openclaw status --deep` (text mode) exits 1 with empty stdout when the deep pass takes longer than the internal health-check budget. The `--json` variant of the same command succeeds at the very same moment, so this is a text/JSON behavioral asymmetry rather than a gateway outage.

## Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.10.9 (8b18b55)`
- Windows 10.0.26200 x64
- Node `24.22.1`

## Reproduction

1. `openclaw status --deep` -> exit code 1, empty stdout.
2. At the same moment, `openclaw status --deep --json` -> exit code 0, normal JSON output.
3. `openclaw status --deep --timeout 600000` -> exit code 0, text output renders normally (took ~217s).

## Actual error

```
Gateway check budget exhausted before health check.
    at resolveStatusGatewayHealth (dist/status-runtime-shared-*.mjs:129)
    at resolveStatusRuntimeSnapshot (dist/status-runtime-shared-*.mjs:196)
    at statusCommand (dist/status.command-*.mjs:69)   // uncaught
```

## Root cause analysis

In `--deep` mode the per-channel probes consume more than the default 60s budget (`GATEWAY_RESTART_REPLACEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS = 6e4`). Once that budget is gone, the health call throws instead of degrading. The JSON path tolerates the exact same condition because it passes `suppressHealthErrors: true` (`dist/status-json-command-*.mjs:132`), while the text path has no equivalent fallback. Result: identical gateway state, two different outcomes depending only on the output format.

## Expected behavior

Either of:

1. Text mode tolerates a health timeout and prints a warning, matching JSON mode; or
2. The default budget adapts to the deep scan duration, and the error message tells the user that `--timeout <ms>` is available.

Verified workarounds today: `--json`, and `--timeout 600000`.

## Is this already fixed upstream?

Checked npm latest **2026.11.3** and it is still not fixed: `text-report-*.mjs:112-120` is structurally identical, `status-runtime-shared-*.mjs:129` still throws, and `status-json-command-*.mjs:133` still passes `true`. So this reproduces on the newest published release as well, not only on the version above.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

In the macOS app on current `main`, the first chat message after a fresh onboarding fails with "This host is low on memory, so it could not start another session." The Mac has plenty of memory. The packaged Gateway runs on Bun, and under Bun `process.availableMemory()` returns only truly free pages, so the 1 GiB Claude CLI live-session guard trips on a healthy Mac.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Build the macOS app from `main` at d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637 (`scripts/package-mac-app.sh`, debug, arm64) and launch it on a fresh profile (`OPENCLAW_PROFILE=onboarding`).
2. Complete onboarding with a local Gateway, using Claude Code (`claude-cli/claude-opus-5-5`) as the AI.
3. Choose **Talk to my agent** and send `hi`.

### Expected behavior

The agent replies. The host was a 48 GB Apple silicon MacBook Pro, and `memory_pressure` reported "System-wide memory free percentage: 70%" at the time.

### Actual behavior

The turn fails before any model call. The chat shows "This host is low on memory, so it could not start another session. Try again after active conversations finish." with Try again / Report a bug.

Gateway log (`~/.openclaw-onboarding/logs/openclaw-onboarding-2026-11-16.log`):

```
lane task error: lane=cli:claude-cli:owner:… durationMs=5 error="Host memory is too low for another CLI live session."
cli terminal failure: provider=claude-cli model=claude-opus-5-5 durationMs=344 … error=Host memory is too low for another CLI live session.
model fallback decision: … reason=rate_limit status=429 code=cli_live_session_host_memory … fallbackStepFinalOutcome=chain_exhausted fallbackConfigured=false
Embedded agent failed before reply: Host memory is too low for another CLI live session.
```

The same Mac, measured with the bundled runtime and with Node at the same moment:

| Runtime | `process.availableMemory()` | `os.freemem()` | `os.totalmem()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bundled Bun 1.4.4 (`~/.openclaw-onboarding/runtime/…/bin/bun`) | 548,831,232 (0.55 GB) | 548,831,232 | 51,539,607,552 |
| Node 26.12.1 | 19,644,563,456 (19.6 GB) | 548,831,232 | — |

Under Bun on macOS, `process.availableMemory()` is identical to `os.freemem()`. macOS keeps truly free pages low, so most Macs in normal use read below 1 GiB.

### OpenClaw version

main d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637 (2026.11.4, app build 2611160101)

### Operating system

macOS 26.5.1 (arm64)

### Install method

mac app (locally packaged from `main`, isolated `OPENCLAW_PROFILE`)

### Model

claude-cli/claude-opus-5-5 (shown in the UI as anthropic/claude-opus-5-5)

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw (mac app, local Gateway on Bun) -> claude-cli live session -> Anthropic

### Additional provider/model setup details

No fallback model configured (fresh onboarding default).

### Logs

See Actual behavior.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Code at the tested commit:

- [`src/infra/host-memory.ts#L8-L14`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637/src/infra/host-memory.ts#L8-L14): `readHostFreeMemoryBytes()` uses `process.availableMemory()` on darwin. Its doc comment assumes Node semantics ("Node's available-memory reading includes inactive and purgeable pages").
- [`src/agents/cli-runner/cli-live-session-registry.ts#L19`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637/src/agents/cli-runner/cli-live-session-registry.ts#L19) and [`#L196-L224`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637/src/agents/cli-runner/cli-live-session-registry.ts#L196-L224): `ensureCliLiveSessionMemory` throws `cli_live_session_host_memory` when that reading is below 1 GiB.
- [`src/agents/failover/user-copy.ts#L66`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637/src/agents/failover/user-copy.ts#L66): user-facing copy.

### Impact and severity

- **Who:** every macOS app user whose first agent runs through the Claude CLI live session. The packaged Gateway always runs on Bun.
- **Severity:** blocks the first message after onboarding. The user is told their Mac is out of memory when it is not. The error is categorized as `rate_limit`/429, so it is retried or reported as capacity instead of a bug.
- **Release exposure:** the guard is on `main` only. It is not in v2026.11.1–v2026.11.3 or v2026.11.5-beta.1. It will ship in the next release cut from `main` unless fixed.

### Additional information

**Contributing changes.** Each change was reasonable on its own; the failure is in how they combine.

1. #161603 (merged 2026-09-30, first shipped in v2026.10.1) moved the macOS app's private runtime, including the local Gateway, to the OpenClaw Bun fork.
2. #144535 (merged 2026-10-10, shipped in v2026.10.10) added `readHostFreeMemoryBytes()` with a macOS branch that relies on Node's `process.availableMemory()`. The app had already been running on Bun for ten days. At that point the only effect was understated free memory in device/host stats.
3. #192534 (merged 2026-11-04, unreleased) added the blocking 1 GiB guard on top of that helper. Its description states the helper reads `process.availableMemory()` on macOS. Its proof simulated memory at the helper/`os.freemem` seam, so the packaged macOS app on Bun was never exercised.

**Process gaps:**
- Nothing tests the host-memory helper under the runtime the macOS app actually ships (Bun). Unit tests mock the reading.
- No packaged-app smoke test sends a first message after a fresh onboarding. A single "fresh install → first reply" check would have caught this before merge.
- The failure maps to `rate_limit`, which hides a local guard decision behind a provider-capacity category.

**Other callers with the same Bun-on-macOS assumption.** These are not user-blocking but read too low under Bun:
- `src/infra/worker-pool-sizing.ts` `resolveUpdateHashWorkerCount()` (`process.availableMemory()`; only Bun on Linux is special-cased).
- `src/commands/doctor-database-port-memory-concurrency.ts` (`readHostFreeMemoryBytes()` → undersized rebuild concurrency).
- `src/gateway/server-methods/system.ts` and `src/node-host/host-stats.ts` (reported free memory).
- `isConstrainedProcessLowOnMemory()` uses `process.constrainedMemory()`; verify its Bun/macOS behavior while fixing.

**Suggested direction:** on darwin, compute reclaimable memory independently of the JS runtime (Mach VM statistics: free + inactive + purgeable + speculative) or detect a Bun-equivalent reading. Cover it with a test that simulates Bun's `availableMemory == freemem` behavior. Optionally, stop classifying this guard as `rate_limit`.

Found during a fresh-install onboarding walkthrough of the macOS app.

issues.body:
I ran into this on #202306 when `checks-node-compact-small-5-2` turned red. Its planner test expected no pre-test build for a selected job, but the planner returned `runtime`. The assertion is what failed the check. [Failed CI job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44715179683/job/136217540190)

I reproduced the same planner bug on clean `main` at `2d7934abf99` using an existing test file. With the GitHub-hosted planner and `OPENCLAW_CI_TEST_RUNTIME_POLICY=bun-all`, I ran this selection against `scripts/lib/ci-node-test-plan.mts`:

```ts
createSelectedNodeTestShardBundles(
  ["src/commands/doctor-auth-canonical-api-key-alias.test.ts"],
  {
    runnerBackend: "github",
    includeReleaseOnlyRuntimeTests: true,
    includePrExemptRuntimeTests: true,
  },
);
```

I expected the job to have no pre-test build because its only selected test has no runtime build prerequisite. The planner emitted `pretestBuildMode: "private-qa"`. A job using that plan would run the extra **Build Node test runtime** step before its tests. I verified the scheduled step from the plan and workflow. Its actual duration and outcome are unmeasured.

I applied the fix locally to #202306’s exact CI merge snapshot, `0b21dde46f3`. The same GitHub-hosted planner assertion passed. I also regenerated the plan and confirmed it still included both selected embedded-agent tests and requested no pre-test build. The fix derives the build mode and its estimated cost from the groups the job will run.

## Summary

I reproduced two UI test failures by delaying the loading of their real, on-demand UI modules. Both tests start polling for rendered content before the relevant module has finished loading.

I reproduced each failure in 3/3 runs without the fix. With the import-completion waits in #204304, each test passed 5/5 runs under the same delayed-loading conditions.

## Steps to reproduce

I tested source at commit `ba2046d48e1784b79121a3de358534df73622760`.

1. In a prepared checkout, create `.openclaw/tmp/ci-flakes/delayed-ui.config.ts` with the configuration below. It reuses the normal UI configuration and delays the selected real module by 1,500 ms.
2. Run the corresponding test command below. The browser test requires the repository's pinned Chromium installation.
3. Apply the corresponding change from #204304 and repeat under the same delayed-loading conditions. Use a fresh filesystem module-cache directory for each login test run.

```ts
import config from "../../../ui/vitest.config.ts";

for (const project of config.test.projects) {
  project.plugins.push({
    name: "ci-flake-delay-lazy-view",
    enforce: "pre",
    async transform(_code, id) {
      if (id.endsWith(process.env.CI_FLAKE_MODULE ?? "/ui/src/lib/toast-view.tsx")) {
        await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 1500));
      }
    },
  });
}

export default config;
```

Login recovery:

```sh
OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=bun \
OPENCLAW_VITEST_FS_MODULE_CACHE_PATH="$PWD/.openclaw/tmp/ci-flakes/cache-delay-base" \
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run \
  --config .openclaw/tmp/ci-flakes/delayed-ui.config.ts \
  ui/src/components/login-gate.test.ts \
  --maxWorkers=1
```

Inline command output:

```sh
CI_FLAKE_MODULE=/ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-tool-expanded.solid.tsx \
OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=bun \
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run \
  --config .openclaw/tmp/ci-flakes/delayed-ui.config.ts \
  ui/src/pages/chat/chat-pane-inline-output.browser.test.tsx \
  --maxWorkers=1
```

## Expected behavior

I expect each test to wait for its real UI module to finish loading before polling for the warning or stdout content. The existing assertions should remain unchanged.

## Actual behavior and results

For login recovery, I observed the reported failure at line 315:

```text
the given combination of arguments (undefined and string) is invalid for this assertion
```

- Without the fix: 3/3 runs failed.
- With the fix: 5/5 full-file runs passed, with all 24 tests passing in each run.
- The change waits for the toast's dynamic import before polling its warning text.

For inline command output, I observed the reported failure at line 212:

```text
expected undefined to be 'First stdout line.'
```

- Without the fix: 3/3 runs failed.
- With the fix: 5/5 runs passed.
- The change moves the existing dynamic-import completion wait before the stdout assertion.

I removed the fixes again after the passing runs, and both failures returned. Those negative-control runs are included in the 3/3 counts above.

## Evidence

- Login recovery CI failure: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45072487555/job/137362837106
- Inline-output CI failure: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/45089601050/job/137416552128
- Proposed fix: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/204304

## Scope and limits

I reproduced the exact assertion failures using controlled delays in real module loading. I did not replay the original full CI shard order or establish that every historical occurrence had the same cause.

I did not replace either renderer with a mock, increase test timeouts, add retries, or weaken assertions. The patch changes only test synchronization. I removed the temporary delay configuration after testing.

issues.body:
When I install a plugin from a Git source pinned to a full commit SHA, the plugin loads, but inspection and the loader report provenance-invalid and warn that OpenClaw cannot verify where it came from.

The installer has correctly saved the source specification, URL, requested ref, resolved commit, and managed installation path.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Create a dependency-free synthetic Git plugin containing package.json, openclaw.plugin.json, and index.cjs.
2. Commit those files and obtain the full commit SHA.
3. In isolated OpenClaw state, run:

pnpm openclaw plugins install "git:file://<absolute-fixture-path>#<full-commit-sha>" --force --accept-capabilities

4. Inspect the installed plugin:

pnpm openclaw plugins inspect <fixture-id> --runtime --json

5. Check the source classification and loader diagnostics.

Expected behavior:

I expect a consistent Git installation record to be recognized as third-party source evidence. Pinning a commit should not grant official-plugin privileges.

Conflicting metadata and mismatched installation ownership should still produce diagnostics.

Actual behavior:

The plugin loads successfully, but I get provenance-invalid and an unverified-source warning.

Cause:

The shared classifier recognizes official installations and consistent third-party npm installations. Otherwise-valid Git installations fall through to provenance-invalid.

Proposed fix:

I want the classifier to check that the saved Git specification, URL, ref, and resolved commit agree, then report third-party-git. A full-SHA pin must match the resolved commit.

The local patch moves the existing source parser into the lightweight source-spec module and updates its callers. That lets source inspection reuse the parser without importing installation orchestration.

Official-plugin privileges and installed-content checks remain unchanged. This is not a workaround.

Environment and evidence:

The reproduction uses main at ba2046d48e1784b79121a3de358534df73622760 in an isolated Linux source checkout, with a generic dependency-free fixture.

The regression exercises real Git, package preparation, managed persistence, inspection, and loader execution. It fails before the fix and passes afterward. The public install and inspection commands were also exercised separately.

Conflicting specification, URL, ref, commit, and installation-path cases still warn. The fixture remains unable to dispatch privileged hook agent turns. The focused parser, installation, and loader trust-diagnostic tests pass.

Impact:

I get a false source-integrity warning for a supported pinned Git installation whose saved records are consistent.

Not checked:

I have not verified remote authenticated Git hosts, Windows runtime behavior, other operating systems, or production deployment.

issues.body:
### Summary

On a Windows Hub node, the Gateway wraps every `exec host=node` command in `cmd.exe /d /s /c`. Because of this wrapper:

- `tools.exec.mode: "auto"` skips the reviewer with `Exec auto-review skipped: dispatch chain cannot be bound`.
- A Gateway allowlist entry for the exact executable path does not match.

So every Windows command needs human approval. There is no middle level between "human approval for each command" and `mode: "full"` for Windows nodes.

### Versions

- Gateway: OpenClaw 2026.9.6 (eb377ac), Linux x64
- Node: Windows Hub 2026.9.4, Windows 11 (10.0.26200)
- Config: `tools.exec.mode: "auto"` with a configured `tools.exec.reviewer.model`

### Steps

1. Run `openclaw approvals allowlist add --agent main "C:\Windows\System32\hostname.exe"`. `openclaw approvals get` shows the entry.
2. From agent `main`, call `exec` with `host: "node"`, `node: "<windows node>"`, `command: "C:\Windows\System32\hostname.exe"`.

### Expected

The allowlist entry matches, or the auto reviewer reviews this plain executable call. The command runs without a human prompt.

### Actual

The tool output contains `Exec auto-review skipped: dispatch chain cannot be bound`. A human approval request is created (`openclaw approvals pending`). If no approval client is online, the run fails with `Headless runs cannot wait for interactive exec approval`.

### Notes

- #114652 made Windows shell startup require human approval so that it cannot bypass auto-review. That is correct for user-supplied wrappers. Here the wrapper comes from the Gateway transport, and the inner command is a single absolute executable path.
- A possible direction: bind and review the inner command for the Gateway's own canonical Windows transport, as the docs describe for "the node's own canonical POSIX shell transport around one direct absolute executable with static arguments".

issues.body:
### Summary

OpenAI-compatible speech cannot deliver its first audio chunk to OpenClaw's streaming TTS callers.

### Problem to solve

Configure the OpenAI speech provider with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that streams the body of `POST /v1/audio/speech`. On current main, a caller using only OpenClaw's streaming TTS API cannot get that stream from the configured provider: the OpenAI speech provider does not implement `streamSynthesize`. The buffered synthesis API must wait until the complete clip is available.

### Proposed solution

Read the guarded audio response incrementally. Use raw PCM when no explicit output format is configured and preserve formats explicitly selected for compatibility endpoints. Let endpoints that return the whole clip deliver it through the same interface. Keep request timeouts, cancellation, response limits, and outbound network policy.

### Alternatives considered

Calling the buffered API per sentence still waits for each complete clip. It is useful for separate playback work but does not repair streaming at the provider boundary.

### Impact

Streaming speech callers cannot use the configured OpenAI-compatible voice with the streaming API even if the endpoint already sends audio in chunks. This issue is about the provider path, not changes to browser Talk playback.

### Evidence/examples

Current main: `extensions/openai/speech-provider.ts` has buffered and telephony synthesis but no streaming hook; `src/tts/tts-streaming.ts` skips providers without that hook. A local regression fixture writes audio and deliberately holds the response open; the streaming caller should receive the first audio before that response closes.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself.

issues.body:
### Summary

`view_image` tool results are persisted verbatim into the agent transcript store, including the full base64 payload of every image. On a single agent this made **352 of 27,706 transcript events (1.3%) account for 451 MB of 564 MB total transcript data (80%)**, driving the agent SQLite database to 1.08 GB and turning routine session writes into 10+ MB synchronous SQLite transactions.

This is the underlying cause of the disk growth reported in #143524 and a major contributor to the main-thread write stalls that precede gateway unresponsiveness.

### Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.3 (1391f7c)
- Windows Server 2022, Node 24.18.0
- Gateway on loopback `127.0.0.1:18789`, single-node install
- Agent store: `%USERPROFILE%\.openclaw\agents\<agent>\agent\openclaw-agent.sqlite`

### Evidence

Event-size distribution across the whole `transcript_events` table for one agent (`javis`):

| single-event size | count | total | share of transcript bytes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| >= 5 MB | 12 | 112.5 MB | 20% |
| 1–5 MB | 122 | 225.8 MB | 40% |
| 256 KB – 1 MB | 218 | 113.1 MB | 20% |
| 64–256 KB | 161 | 25.6 MB | 5% |
| < 64 KB | 27,193 | 87.0 MB | 15% |

So **1.3% of events hold 80% of the bytes**, while the 27,193 ordinary conversational events total only 87 MB.

Every one of the largest events is the same shape — a `toolResult` from `view_image` whose `content` is raw base64:

```
--- 11.8MB session=c8b426bb seq=49 ---
{"type":"message","id":"75260f9f-...","timestamp":"2026-09-04T09:49:44.545Z",
 "message":{"role":"toolResult","toolCallId":"call_9vfbipmasjja4bn7j6emq9kx",
 "toolName":"view_image","content": ...
mid-payload sample: xsoB+oBfgF7WR20gANqGogc8/T3epIoeA9POnVANZ7gCGIA9NR8wfXzNcdZhbVIBxoBVtWq1wRdSx+us/S34...
```

Top offenders (same agent, all `toolName: "view_image"`):

| session | size | events | bytes/event | largest single event |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `c8b426bb` | 46.5 MB | 59 | 807 KB | 11.8 MB |
| `90a3362d` | 39.6 MB | 34 | 1192 KB | 11.3 MB |
| `17ab66fa` | 21.9 MB | 99 | 227 KB | 10.4 MB |
| `f6ff53d2` | 17.4 MB | 79 | 226 KB | 6.7 MB |

For contrast, a genuinely long text conversation in the same store is `967b2361` — 47.2 MB across **4,633** events (10 KB/event, evenly distributed). That is normal usage. The image sessions reach comparable size in **34–59 events**.

Reproduction is simply: send several images to an agent over Feishu/WeChat so `view_image` runs, then query the store:

```sql
SELECT session_id, COUNT(*) ev,
       SUM(LENGTH(event_json)) bytes,
       MAX(LENGTH(event_json)) biggest
FROM transcript_events
GROUP BY session_id
ORDER BY bytes DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Each `view_image` call adds roughly (image bytes × 1.33) to the transcript, permanently.

### Impact

1. **Store size** — 1.3% of events produce 80% of the bytes. This is the mechanism behind the 1.4–2.8 GB WAL growth in #143524; the WAL is large because the rows being written are large.
2. **Synchronous write latency** — persisting a single 11 MB event is one synchronous SQLite transaction on the gateway's main thread. On this host that showed up as `slow SQLite transaction hold` warnings with `elapsedMs` from 1,205 up to 68,000, and correlates with the gateway going unresponsive while `node.exe` stays alive and the port stops accepting connections.
3. **Retention cannot recover it** — `openclaw sessions cleanup --enforce` with `pruneAfter=7d` / `maxEntries=2000` pruned 50 entries and freed **53 KB**, because the bulk sits inside recently-active sessions protected by `preserveRecent`. Deleting five image-heavy sessions removed 135.8 MB of transcript data (564.0 → 428.2 MB) but the file grew 1075.9 → 1084.3 MB with only 72.8 MB freelist, so reclaiming it further requires offline `VACUUM`.
4. **`VACUUM` is not a remedy** — a full offline `VACUUM` before any deletion took **406 s** and recovered **4 MB** (1079.3 → 1075.4 MB, freelist 0). The data is live, not fragmentation.

### Expected behaviour

Image payloads should not be stored inline in the transcript. Reasonable options, roughly in order of preference:

1. **Store by reference.** Persist images as content-addressed blobs on disk (the `sessions/` directory already holds per-session artifacts) and keep only a path/hash plus metadata in `transcript_events`.
2. **Cap persisted tool-result size.** Truncate any single tool result above a configurable threshold (e.g. `session.maintenance.maxEventBytes`) when writing to the store, keeping the model-visible payload in memory for the current turn only.
3. **Strip base64 on persist.** The base64 is only needed for the in-flight model call; after the turn completes it has no replay value that a stored file path would not serve better.
4. **At minimum, make it visible.** Emit a warning when a single transcript event exceeds a few MB, and count inline-media bytes in the `diskBudget` report so operators can see where the growth comes from.

### Related

- #143524 — WAL growth on agent SQLite (this issue is the likely root cause of the volume)
- #143757 — Windows scheduled-task config prevents headless gateway start (separate defect on the same host)

### Notes

Happy to run additional queries against this store — it still contains 428 MB of transcript data with the pattern intact, and the deleted sessions are preserved as `.zst` archives under `agents/javis/sessions/` if a before/after comparison is useful.

issues.body:
**What happens.** On Windows, managed llama.cpp setup (`@openclaw/llama-cpp-provider` 2026.10.10-beta.5, and the same table in 2026.10.10 and on main) fails closed with `download SHA-256 mismatch: expected 8c79a9b226de4b3cacfd1f83d24f962d0773be79f1e7b75c6af4ded7e32ae1d6, got 3210c429...` on an NVIDIA CUDA host, reproducibly. The integrity check is doing its job: the bytes served are not the published asset.

**Why.** `extensions/llama-cpp/src/llama-server-assets.ts` pins `LLAMA_SERVER_RELEASE = "b10809"` and downloads from `https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/releases/download/b10809/<name>`. GitHub's release metadata for b10809 still lists the published size and digest (e.g. `cudart-llama-bin-win-cuda-12.4-x64.zip`, 391443627 bytes, `sha256:8c79a9b2...`, unchanged since 2026-09-04), but the asset storage now answers with a much shorter body. `HEAD` on the redirected download, 2026-11-03:

| asset (b10809) | published | served |
|---|---|---|
| cudart-llama-bin-win-cuda-12.4-x64.zip | 391443627 | 6491 |
| cudart-llama-bin-win-cuda-13.3-x64.zip | 390970417 | 6491 |
| llama-b10809-bin-win-cuda-13.3-x64.zip | 149558056 | 2547 |
| llama-b10809-bin-win-cpu-x64.zip | 18407457 | 507 |
| llama-b10809-bin-win-cpu-arm64.zip | 11974499 | 371 |

The other 22 b10809 assets (macOS, Linux, the Windows CUDA 12.4 server zip) are served at full length. So every managed Windows setup the table can select fails: CUDA 12.4 x64 (its cudart dependency), CUDA 13.3 x64 (its cudart and server zip), CPU x64 and CPU arm64 (the server zip).

**Suggested fix.** Move the managed runtime to a llama.cpp build whose Windows assets are served at their published size (b11500 and b12074 both are, and carry the identical cudart zip, same digest), with the usual version/commit and per-asset digests from that release's metadata. Optionally pass each asset's `sizeBytes` as `expectedSize` (today only the VC runtime gets it), so a short body fails as a size mismatch that names the source rather than as a hash mismatch.

We did not swap the pinned digest: the check must keep failing closed.

## Summary
A long-running task can stop making progress even though its command is still running and helpers have completed their work. The assistant's intentional pause is falsely marked as a failure; subsequent user follow-ups and helper-result deliveries can then be rejected because the same background work is still running.

This is not just a misleading error message: the assistant cannot receive the results it needs to continue, and asking it to continue can hit another error instead of recovering the task.

The trigger is a silent Codex turn with a confirmed retained background command: it fails with a missing-tool-result error even though the command is correctly recorded as still running.

## User-facing impact
In the observed long-running Discord workflow:

- Work that should have continued automatically stalled after an intentional pause.
- Completed helper results failed to reach the main assistant, so completed work did not advance the task.
- Attempts to continue were rejected with an instruction to stop the running work and retry. That puts the user in the position of being told to interrupt legitimate work just to regain a responsive assistant.

From the user's perspective, the assistant breaks precisely when a substantial task needs coordination: background work is running, results are ready, but the assistant cannot take the next step or reliably accept a follow-up. The user has to intervene and troubleshoot the assistant instead of receiving the requested outcome.

The false missing-result classification is reproduced deterministically. The continuation and delivery failures were observed in the live workflow and match the retention/cleanup path described below; the tests do not recreate that entire live cascade. There is no evidence here of firmware corruption or failure of the running command itself.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Run a Codex-backed turn that starts a native command and leaves it running.
2. Let the turn finish silently while that command is confirmed by `thread/backgroundTerminals/list`.
3. Observe the terminal error and attempt to continue while background work is retained.

The paired PR adds a deterministic adapter regression using `NO_REPLY` and a confirmed background-terminal inventory. It does not require live inference.

## Expected behavior
A confirmed retained command keeps its neutral running record without making the turn fail. Genuine missing results must still fail.

## Actual behavior
The running command receives a nonerror “still running” result, but `synthesizeMissingToolResults` also includes its ID in the missing-result error count:

> OpenClaw recorded a native Codex tool.call without a matching tool.result before the turn completed.

In an observed long-running session, this was followed by failed continuation/helper-result deliveries with:

> Codex thread <thread-id> still has background work after waiting for cleanup; stop its running work and retry.

The source path explains the connection: the false prompt error prevents normal completed-turn retention; a subsequent cold resume cannot release protected background work. Not every occurrence of the latter error is necessarily this bug.

## Environment
OpenClaw and Codex plugin 2026.11.2; Codex app-server 0.164.0; npm global install; macOS 27.2 (Apple Silicon); Node 26.13.0. Native Codex/OpenAI route. The deterministic reproduction is model-independent.

## Additional information
The defect is also present on main at f615e96b55becb3944b57de4e8af74a801814fab. #156764 added the neutral retained-command record, but its regression supplied a final answer and did not cover silent turns. #194757 addresses a separate continuation path; this report concerns missing-result classification.

issues.body:
# Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash). Not known to be a regression: we did not test Components V2 edits on any earlier version.

# Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

The Discord `message` tool `edit` action cannot edit a message that was sent with Components V2 (`flags & IS_COMPONENTS_V2`, 1<<15). The agent-facing `editMessage` handler hard-requires `content`, ignores any `components` param, and always PATCHes a body containing `content`. Discord rejects `content` on a Components V2 message, so the edit fails with `Invalid Form Body`. Without `content` the tool rejects the call before reaching Discord. There is no agent path to update an interactive card in place (e.g. flip a card to "approved" after a button click).

The plugin already has the right primitive — `editDiscordComponentMessage()` (`extensions/discord/src/send.components.ts`, via `writeDiscordComponentMessage(to, spec, opts, messageId)`), used internally by the outbound adapter and the plugin-binding approval flow — but the `editMessage` action never routes to it.

Handler, `extensions/discord/src/actions/runtime.messaging.messages.ts` (unchanged on `main` @ 0d9e310d9f):

```ts
case "editMessage": {
  ...
  const content = snapshot
    ? (buildDiscordTextChunks(/* progress draft */)[0] ?? "")
    : readStringParam(ctx.params, "content", {
        required: true,
        allowEmpty: true,
        trim: false,
      });
  await ctx.assertReadTargetAllowed({ channelId });
  const message = await editMessageDiscord(channelId, messageId, {
    content,
    ...(snapshot ? { allowedMentions: { parse: [] } } : {}),
  }, ctx.withOpts());
```

Shipped bundle 2026.9.8, `editMessageDiscord` (`send.messages.ts`):

```js
async function editMessageDiscord(channelId, messageId, payload, opts) {
  const rest = resolveDiscordRest(opts);
  return await editChannelMessage(rest, channelId, messageId, { body: {
    content: payload.content,
    ...payload.flags !== void 0 ? { flags: payload.flags } : {},
    ...payload.allowedMentions ? { allowed_mentions: payload.allowedMentions } : {}
  } });
}
```

`content` is always present in the body, and `components` is never forwarded.

## Steps to reproduce

1. From an agent in a Discord channel, send a card with the `message` tool using `components` (Components V2 container + buttons). Note its message id.
2. In the same conversation, call `message` with `action: "edit"`, `messageId`, `message: "<new text>"` and a new `components` payload.
3. Call it again with only `components` (no `message`/`content`).

## Expected behavior

`edit` with `components` rebuilds the Components V2 payload and PATCHes it (same path as `editDiscordComponentMessage`), omitting `content`. An edit that carries only text on a V2 message either fails with a clear tool error or is converted into a text display component.

## Actual behavior

Measured 2026-10-05 on message 1556671249827111104 in a guild text channel:

- step 2 (`message` + `components`) → `DiscordError: Invalid Form Body` (Discord refuses `content` on a message flagged IS_COMPONENTS_V2; `components` was dropped by the handler).
- step 3 (`components` only) → `ToolInputError: content required` (`readStringParam(..., "content", { required: true })`).

## Environment

- openclaw 2026.9.8 (npm global), `@openclaw/discord` 2026.9.8 (npm plugin)
- Linux 7.0.14 x64, Node 24.21.0
- Model: anthropic/claude-opus-5-5 (irrelevant to the defect)

## Provider / routing chain

agent → `message` tool `action: "edit"` → Discord plugin `handleAction` → `editMessage` case → `editMessageDiscord` → `PATCH /channels/{id}/messages/{id}`.

## Additional setup details

No local patch on the Discord plugin or its dist. A separate, by-design gate (`Delegated discord:edit requires the exact current conversation and account for this plugin`) blocks the edit from a session outside the card's conversation; that is not part of this report.

## Impact and severity

Interactive cards (approve/deny buttons) cannot change state after a click: the card keeps showing live buttons for an already-resolved decision, and the only workaround is posting a new message, which duplicates the card in the channel. This blocks our actionable-cards contract amendment that makes a card reflect its resolved state.

Suggested fix shape: in `editMessage`, when `components` (or `blocks`) is present, build the spec the same way `sendMessage` does and call `editDiscordComponentMessage`; make `content` optional in that branch.

issues.body:
## Summary

`openclaw gateway restart` reports a hard failure on restarts that actually succeed, and **exits 0 while doing so**. The readiness budget it enforces is hardcoded to 60 s, which is shorter than a real cold start of this gateway, so the CLI times out on a service that comes up healthy a minute later.

There is no flag to raise the budget: `--wait` controls the delay *before* restarting, not the post-restart readiness timeout.

## Version / platform

- OpenClaw 2026.9.6 (eb377ac, npm latest)
- macOS 26 / arm64, Node 26.8.1
- LaunchAgent-managed gateway (`gui/501/ai.openclaw.gateway`), `--max-old-space-size=6144`
- Config `/Users/jiang/.openclaw/openclaw.json`, bind loopback, port 18789

## The budget

`gateway-shutdown-budget.mjs`:

```js
// Shared stop policy; v2026.9.5 restart-health.constants.ts fixes the replacement window.
export const GATEWAY_RESTART_REPLACEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS = 60_000;
export const GATEWAY_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS = 315_000;
```

and `dist/restart-health.constants-*.mjs` derives the probe budget directly from it:

```js
const DEFAULT_RESTART_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_MS = GATEWAY_RESTART_REPLACEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS;   // 60_000
const DEFAULT_RESTART_HEALTH_ATTEMPTS = Math.ceil(DEFAULT_RESTART_HEALTH_TIMEOUT_MS / 500);
```

So the health budget is the shutdown budget constant, reused verbatim. 60 s is not configurable from the CLI — `gateway restart --help` exposes only `--force`, `--json`, `--preserve-definition`, `--safe`, `--skip-deferral`, `--wait`, and none of them adjust the readiness timeout.

## Reproduction

Observed cold starts of this gateway (measured by polling `/healthz` + `/readyz` every 5 s from a separate shell):

| Run | Elapsed to `healthz=200` **and** `readyz=200` |
|---|---|
| 1 | 70 s |
| 2 | 75 s |
| 3 | 75 s |
| 4 | 200 s |

Every one of these is a successful start. The 200 s run is presumably a slow catalog/plugin warm-up, but the point is that the spread is wide and unbounded from below the user's perspective — a fixed 60 s budget will miss part of the distribution.

Actual `openclaw gateway restart` output from the run above:

```
Restarted LaunchAgent: gui/501/ai.openclaw.gateway
Timed out after 98s waiting for gateway port 18789 to become healthy.
Readiness budget exhausted after 98s. Last observed startup phase: waiting for Gateway health and identity.
Service runtime: status=running, state=active, pid=65913
Port 18789 is already in use.
- pid 65913 jiang: /opt/homebrew/opt/node/bin/node --max-old-space-size=6144 ... (127.0.0.1:18789)
Gateway probe failed: gateway timeout after 3000ms
Gateway target: ws://127.0.0.1:18789
Gateway restart timed out after 98s waiting for health checks.
Tip: openclaw gateway status --deep
Tip: openclaw doctor
```

Total wall time: 121 s. The service came up and served requests normally immediately afterwards (`healthz=200`, `readyz=200`, and the log shows successful `ws` traffic on the same pid 65913).

Two separate problems are visible in that output:

**1. The false failure.** The service was `status=running, state=active, pid=65913` and the port was bound by *the new process*, yet the CLI still concluded "timed out". The health probe that failed was a 3 s `ws` connect attempt, which is a much stricter criterion than the service being up.

**2. `exit 0` on failure.** The command printed a timeout error and a stack of "Tip:" lines, then **exited 0**. Any wrapper script or automation that checks the exit status will treat a failed restart as a success. This is the more dangerous half of the bug — it is what let a nightly restart silently do nothing for 8 hours on my host before I noticed.

## Suggested fixes

- Exit non-zero when the readiness budget is exhausted, regardless of the underlying service state
- Either raise `GATEWAY_RESTART_REPLACEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS`, or derive it from `GATEWAY_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS` (315 s) the way the drain budget already is, or expose a `--health-timeout <ms>` flag
- Distinguish "service is not running" from "service is running but slow to become ready" — the latter should not be reported as a restart failure, and the `Port 18789 is already in use` line is misleading here, since the process holding the port *is* the replacement

## Workaround

Drive `launchd` directly (`launchctl bootout gui/501/ai.openclaw.gateway` + `launchctl bootstrap gui/501 <plist>`) and poll readiness yourself with a larger budget. Note that `bootout` is asynchronous — bootstrapping immediately afterwards fails with `Bootstrap failed: 5: Input/output error`, so the replacement needs a wait-and-retry loop. That part works reliably and is what I use for a scheduled daily restart.

issues.body:
## Current proposal and maintainer decision

This scope incorporates the later [narrowed author proposal](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/159743#issuecomment-5933165699) and [ownership decision request](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/159743#issuecomment-6345735773). It supersedes the original repair/default-on aspirations retained below. Maintainer sponsorship and ownership remain open.

Provide an opt-in observation window attached to an existing update-run identity. Baseline only updater/managed-service executable identity and version, state-schema compatibility, and configured scheduler job identities/next eligible run times in contexts the installation already manages. Observe each eligible job’s first actual post-cutover run using existing scheduler facts; no arbitrary-shell discovery, bespoke capability probes, forced runs or test messages. The proposed finite default is 72 hours, with a fixed cutover/deadline retained across restart; at expiry, jobs without an eligible run remain unobserved. Retain one local, redacted status projection. The stale-CLI example below is historical motivation, not a demonstrated current-main regression.

- Separate execution, completion and delivery evidence. A successful process exit alone does not prove output or delivery.
- Keep not-yet-due work pending and absent capabilities skipped. Missing evidence remains unverified.
- Preserve existing ownership of update execution, scheduler state and application data. No repairs, restarts, migrations, rollback or task mutations belong to this first slice.
- Use a fixed deadline that restarts do not extend; eligible work not observed by expiry remains unobserved. Retain a local redacted status projection and surface actionable changes without repeated success notifications.

**Decision requested:** would a maintainer sponsor a narrow core-owned read-only update-lifecycle contract consumed by an optional observer, with retained status owned by existing update history? If a core implementation is preferred, please identify that route and the retained-status owner. These are recommended ownership/default choices, not approval or a new implementation claim.

<details>
<summary>Original proposal retained for history — superseded scope</summary>

# [Feature]: Installation-aware post-upgrade survey and monitored recovery window

## Summary

After an OpenClaw upgrade, automatically inventory the installation's enabled capabilities, run a bounded health survey for several days, and surface actionable regressions with safe repair options. An upgrade should not be considered healthy solely because the gateway restarted once.

## Problem to solve

Customized installations have more moving parts than a single startup canary: scheduler jobs, model/provider routes, plugins, channels, memory indexes, SQLite state, Workboard, dashboards, service launchers, and scripts that resolve the CLI through different paths. Failures may appear only when a scheduled job next runs or a less-used feature is invoked. Operators therefore spend days remembering and manually checking every corner after each upgrade.

One concrete failure mode: the running installation and state database had advanced, but an older `openclaw` executable still won in some shell/scheduled PATHs. That executable rejected the newer database schema, breaking otherwise read-only Workboard and scheduled health checks. A startup success alone did not reveal those paths.

## Proposed solution

Add an opt-in (or clearly announced default-on) **post-upgrade observation window** tied to the upgrade transaction:

1. **Discover the actual installation before changing it.** Build a redacted capability manifest from enabled/configured components and executable resolution in relevant contexts (interactive shell, managed service, scheduled-command environment). Record a pre-upgrade baseline of versions, database schema, configured jobs and next-run times, plugin load status, channel connection state, model-route probes where enabled, memory/index health, and Workboard availability. Allow user-defined read-only probes for bespoke integrations.
2. **Run dependency-aware checks after cutover.** Perform immediate preflight and post-start checks, then periodic checks for a configurable 48–72 hours and after each enabled scheduled job's first due run. Include CLI/schema compatibility, gateway and channel health, scheduler execution *and expected output/receipt*, plugin diagnostics, model/auth routes, database integrity, memory searches, Workboard reads, and configured dashboard/report freshness. Skip unconfigured capabilities rather than reporting them as broken.
3. **Compare against baseline, not just absolute green/red.** Detect missing jobs, changed CLI targets, new failures, lost output, stale reports, and regressions in previously working features. Distinguish a failing check from a check that has not yet had a chance to run. Coalesce repeated symptoms into one incident with probable dependency/root cause and affected components.
4. **Offer bounded recovery.** Automatically retry safe read-only checks and reversible local repairs when explicitly configured; generate a preview for config/plugin/CLI-path fixes. Require approval for external sends, card/task mutations, database migration or rollback, service restarts, and other consequential changes. Verify the original failing probe after a repair. Never downgrade a newer state database to make an older CLI work.
5. **Produce one durable upgrade health view.** Show coverage, latest evidence, pending first-run checks, active regressions, attempted repairs, and the end of the observation window in CLI and UI. Alert only on new/actionable changes or deadline misses, not on every successful poll. Redact secrets and private content from diagnostics and exported support bundles.

Suggested CLI surface (illustrative): `openclaw update monitor status --json`, `openclaw update monitor run --read-only`, and `openclaw update monitor export --redacted`. The survey should not require operators to maintain a hard-coded checklist for every built-in capability.

## Acceptance criteria

- An upgrade with a deliberately stale CLI first in one scheduled PATH flags the path/version/schema mismatch even when the gateway is healthy.
- A scheduled job that reports success but produces no expected artifact/receipt is reported as unverified or degraded, not healthy.
- A feature that has not yet reached its next scheduled run stays pending; a feature absent from the manifest is skipped.
- A previously working Workboard read or plugin load that fails after upgrade is reported with its first failing probe and version transition.
- One root-cause incident can group cascading failures without hiding each affected capability.
- No channel messages, Workboard mutations, schema downgrades, or destructive repair occur as part of observation or without the appropriate approval.
- Monitoring ends (or explicitly transitions to normal monitoring) after the configured window and retains a concise, redacted result.

## Alternatives considered

`doctor` and a one-time post-update canary are useful but cannot see delayed scheduled failures or bespoke paths. Site-specific shell scripts and dashboard panels can fill gaps, but force every operator to rediscover coverage after every release and provide no common baseline or lifecycle.

## Impact

Affected: operators with multi-agent or customized OpenClaw installations. Severity: recurring operational disruption after upgrades. Frequency: each substantial upgrade, with failures often delayed by job cadence. Consequence: days of manual surveillance, stale reports, broken automation, and avoidable operator intervention.

## Evidence/examples

- Related but narrower: #154605 (upgrade stability/version mismatches), #142580 (green upgrade with lost continuity), #134570 (incomplete migration and silent dispatch failures), #98753 (health/cron CLI failure).
- Local observation: OpenClaw 2026.9.2 supported state schema through 15 while the live database was schema 18; OpenClaw 2026.9.6 could perform the equivalent read-only checks. CLI resolution differed by execution context.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only.


</details>

issues.body:
## Summary

After upgrading a multi-agent macOS Gateway from OpenClaw 2026.9.2 to 2026.9.6 (`eb377ac`), fresh non-delivering Codex-backed agent turns intermittently fail before producing a reply. Two observed failure classes are:

```text
prepared model runtime publication was superseded for <agent-dir>
codex app-server request timed out | codex app-server initialize timed out | CODEX_APP_SERVER_STARTUP_CANCELLED
```

The Gateway and auxiliary services remain reachable, so transport health checks alone do not catch the lost inference. The issue affects multiple agents rather than a single model alias or meeting job.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.6 (`eb377ac`), upgraded from 2026.9.2
- macOS Apple Silicon, Node v24.16.0
- npm installation; Gateway runs under an existing macOS LaunchAgent with a nonstandard NVM Node path
- Codex runtime with named OpenAI Sol, Terra, and Luna model routes
- Approximately 100 enabled cron jobs across multiple agents

The service and Node path were checked against the existing LaunchAgent; no Node or package ambiguity was found.

## Observations

1. The 2026.9.6 package/config validated and model-status checks for sampled agents showed usable OpenAI profiles, zero missing providers, and zero route issues.
2. After one fresh Gateway start, coding-sysadmin (Sol) returned the publication-superseded error; coding-sysadmin and code-op-nuclear (Terra) also returned Codex app-server request timeouts.
3. A second operator-approved guarded restart, with no package or model-routing change, brought the same existing Gateway label back. Fresh non-delivering simple turns then yielded:
   - main / Sol: success (`OK`)
   - science-writer / Sol: publication-superseded error
   - worker / Luna: app-server initialize/request timeout with `CODEX_APP_SERVER_STARTUP_CANCELLED`
   - coding-sysadmin / Sol: publication-superseded error
   - code-op-nuclear / Terra: app-server initialize/request timeout
4. The live config hash and mtime did not change during these tests. No automatic config rewrite or hot reload trigger was observed. The Gateway process remained the sole listener on its port. Gateway HTTP/RPC, the report endpoint, and the A2A agent card responded successfully; Telegram probe also reported running/OK.
5. Before the second restart, multiple isolated jobs across agents ended in prepared reply-dispatch/runtime-owner errors. Only one scheduled heartbeat had run after the second restart at the time of this report, and it succeeded; no claim is made that the pre-restart job failure count measures post-restart reliability.
6. There are frequent `models.list` calls from existing control UI clients, and provider catalog refreshes sometimes coincide with app-server timeouts. This is a correlation only. `status --deep --json` sampled after the second restart showed modelCatalog worker `activeTasks:0`, `pendingTasks:0`; the perpetual catalog rebuild described in #157107 was not observed in that sample.

A narrow termination of one verified idle app-server child before the restarts did not fix the affected agent; it was not repeated. No Doctor, onboarding, model-policy change, broad process kill, or SentinelOne change was used.

## Investigation status (October 1, 2026)

Following the [ClawSweeper review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/158127#issuecomment-5833021330), this report tracks two separate failure boundaries:

- **Runtime publication admission:** `prepared model runtime publication was superseded` can reject a turn before model execution. Subsequent operator reports include non-Codex routes, so this path is not Codex-specific. OAuth adoption, catalog refresh, and scheduling overlap remain candidate triggers rather than an established shared cause.
- **Codex startup/acquisition:** initialize/request timeouts and startup cancellation occur before native turn execution. Our previously posted matched probes and native-log observations narrow this boundary; they do not prove a publication race causes it.

The [new per-agent auth-reload report](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/158127#issuecomment-5875956290) provides a useful cold-start hypothesis for the second path. In our retained September 25 macOS observations, however, repeated auth-reload and remote-control preference messages appeared for both the failing auxiliary agent and the successful main-agent control. Those messages alone therefore do not distinguish our failure; their timing relative to initialization, auth application, catalog requests, and app-server generation needs correlation.

No deterministic reproduction against current main or recovery on a newer release has been established by the reporter. This update reviews retained evidence only; it includes no fresh production probe, restart, or configuration/auth change. The next evidence needed is a separately attributable admission trace for publication supersession and a startup trace for Codex acquisition. A blanket cron retry or copying auth files would not establish either cause.

## Expected

A fresh agent turn should acquire the current published runtime and complete or report a specific provider/auth error. A timed-out app-server initialization should be isolated and recoverable without repeated Gateway restarts or loss of unrelated agents' turns.

## Impact

Scheduled work and agent replies are at risk while the Gateway appears healthy. Two meeting-report inputs remain missing, and consolidation was held to avoid treating partial output as complete. The operator is keeping the partly functional Gateway running rather than taking down reports, A2A, and Telegram while investigating.

## Related reports

- #156975 has the exact `prepared model runtime publication was superseded` error on 2026.9.6, but focuses on fallback/error presentation on another platform.
- #139830 and #139710 report the related but different `plugin generation was superseded` error.
- #84567 and #80618 describe older Codex initialization/concurrency hangs.
- #157107 describes a 2026.9.6 catalog-worker loop; the sampled worker state here does not establish that loop.

Sanitized evidence is available; this is an observed production failure, not a deterministic minimal reproduction. AI-assisted investigation and report prepared with Codex.

## Problem
The team-mode Control UI sidebar has no manual agent section order. Operators cannot keep their frequently used agents near the top without changing unrelated agent configuration.

## Proposed behavior
Add drag-and-drop and keyboard-accessible Move up / Move down controls to team-sidebar agent headers, moving the entire agent section with its children. Reuse the existing sidebar header grip, interactive-control guards, header-midpoint before/after insertion feedback and array-move helper. Provide Reset agent order.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Crash (process/app exits or hangs)

### Summary

`$include` resolution now walks documents on an explicit work stack (stack-safe), but the config-loading stages that run **after** include resolution still recurse over the resolved value. A config whose nested value survives include resolution crashes one of the later stages with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`, so the operator sees an opaque CLI/Gateway crash instead of a clean schema rejection.

Three recursion points sit on the resolved-value path:

1. `src/infra/deep-merge.ts` — `mergeDeep` and `sanitizePlainObject` clone/walk the resolved tree recursively.
2. `src/config/env-substitution.ts` — `substituteAny` walks containers recursively while substituting `${...}` values.
3. Legacy migration probes — load-time `structuredClone(root)` calls (Node's built-in clone is itself recursive) in the legacy config migration probes.

### Steps to reproduce

`deep-config.json` (generated with a script, 4000 levels):

```json
{ "x": { "x": { ... nested 4000 times ... } } }
```

`openclaw.json`:

```json
{ "$include": "./deep-config.json" }
```

```bash
OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH=./openclaw.json pnpm openclaw config read
# → read failed: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

The include resolver itself accepts the document (it is stack-safe), then the crash happens later in the load chain. Catching the exact stage: patch the `catch` in the config io snapshot path with `process._rawDebug(e.stack)` and run the CLI sources via `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs` (the installed CLI runs dist, which predates any local change).

### Expected behavior

A deeply nested config is either rejected with the normal, actionable schema error (`Unrecognized key` / validation message) or handled iteratively — not an opaque stack-overflow crash from a stage after the one that already promises stack safety.

### Actual behavior

`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` from deep-merge, env substitution, or a migration-probe clone, depending on how far the load chain gets.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.5 / current main

### Operating system

Linux

### Install method

pnpm (repo checkout)
