prs.title: feat(webui): add session-scoped reasoning effort
prs.body:
## Why

Tracking: [NAN-355](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-355).

Choose reasoning effort for the next message in one conversation without opening settings, modifying a shared preset, or changing a task that is already running. A click should not create a conversation or synchronize a separate server-side setting.

## What changed

- Reuse the preset editor's existing model catalog and recommendation helper. Chat offers click-only choices; there is no second capability policy or free-text field.
- Update the browser preference immediately and coalesce browser-storage writes for 250 ms. Sending takes the latest value synchronously, without a reasoning save request, acknowledgement, or first-message save barrier.
- Carry the optional effort in the ordinary message. The existing trusted WebUI admission transaction remembers the last-used value in session metadata; execution derives an independent generation snapshot. Preset changes clear the override. Shell/restart/other non-generating control commands retain their existing behavior.
- Remove the dedicated reasoning service, HTTP read/mutation, WebSocket settings action, scope/config signature, and prototype session-header API. Drop the shared segmented control's now-unused pending-save extension.
- Preserve the accepted compact menu, neutral provider icons, selected-row shading/shadow, aligned control edges, inset corners, and narrow-screen touch targets.

## Scope

A selected-but-unsent preference belongs to this browser. The last-used value is saved only with ordinary message admission, and is restored through the existing session list/attach projection after a Gateway restart. No config/preset write, new lock or settings synchronization subsystem is added. The optional `webui.reasoning-effort.v1` flag advertises message support to the UI; temporary chats do not expose this shortcut.

Omitted message effort preserves the saved session/preset value; explicit null follows the preset; native `none` remains a string. The gateway validates trusted generating input, rather than treating the recommendation list as a new authorization or provider-compatibility policy. Existing authentication and temporary-chat ownership checks remain in place.

## Tradeoffs

Recommendations intentionally match the preset editor, including its fallback recommendations. They are not real-generation capability probes or a guarantee that every upstream API accepts each value or gives it a distinct meaning. Existing provider serialization and request-body precedence are unchanged. Unreleased prototype hash-dict session metadata is not migrated.

## Blast Radius

The existing WebUI message admission and per-execution generation snapshot; existing session metadata/list/attach projection; model-menu local preference, first-message transfer, and send options. Regression checks cover token renewal, session/host isolation, preserving a newer target choice, preset switching, and ordinary shell/restart controls. No execution lifecycle, queue architecture, provider protocol, TUI, or deployment redesign is included.

## Verification

- Backend: 223 targeted mock/temporary-data tests passed; touched Ruff and import boundaries passed. The tested backend patch hash was checked against the final candidate.
- Frontend: final hook/menu/segmented-control/thread-shell set passed (135 tests), plus targeted transport, attachment, composer/model-menu tests and the preset-picker recommendation case. Overlapping test runs are not summed. TypeScript, touched ESLint, independent production build, and diff check passed.
- Isolated real Gateway + Chromium + loopback fake provider: clicking on a blank topic did not mutate session/config or send a settings action; latest effort reached the first model request; assistant responses and explicit turn-end events were persisted; another topic remained unchanged; in-flight effort stayed fixed; queued editing/resending and cancellation used the expected values; actual Gateway process restarts preserved both browser-local unsent choice and session last-used choice in a fresh browser. Desktop/320px, light/dark geometry checks confirmed aligned edges and 44px narrow-screen targets.
- Build assets and HOME/config/workspace/sessions were independent. Config bytes stayed unchanged; no real model, credential, daily instance, or handed-off preview was used or operated.
- Follow-up HEAD: `2fa444817f8232fec1b8bd706aeb5eb90f508b35` (normal commit/push). GitHub currently reports this Draft PR as `CONFLICTING` / `DIRTY`; the new head has no check rollup or workflow run. Exact-head remote CI is therefore not verified. No rebase, force-push, or base-merge was performed without authorization.

## Verification limits

Real providers, Safari, physical devices, and a full local suite were not tested. Very early Escape during menu opening was timing-sensitive in initial browser attempts; its cause is not established. Loaded-menu checks wait for the ordinary lazy catalog response and pass; no speculative Escape fallback was added. This remains a Draft PR, not an approval, Ready transition, merge, or deployment.

prs.title: perf(webui): batch startup recovery and authenticate before React
prs.body:
## Why

Opening WebUI should make a conversation usable quickly, not merely paint a placeholder. **Draft: the recovery and desktop history improvements are real, but the end-to-end target is not met.** In the mixed navigation run, the desktop new-chat command took longer to be acknowledged.

## What changed

- The launcher validates the same WebSocket config without loading the listener or the foreground agent runtime. The gateway batches both restart scans; checkpoints, pending follow-ups, interrupted transcripts and child tasks are still handled before admission.
- The browser starts one same-origin, no-store bootstrap before loading React, translations and chat. The initial static JavaScript needed to start authentication fell from 248 kB to 3.75 kB (gzip). Chat controls remain behind successful authentication.

## Tradeoffs

Keep the draft open until the desktop send regression is understood. Profile chat creation, catalog refresh and the server acknowledgement separately; the existing-chat route also still waits for the full session list. A cached PWA launch and remote/native latency were not measured. No new background service, auth shortcut or data migration is introduced.

## Verification

Windows, production assets, same Python/Chromium. Restored one consistent **2.45 GiB** database snapshot (**1,012 sessions, 340 WebUI chats**) per process. Five paired runs per version with the order alternated; fresh browser contexts, HTTP cache disabled, service worker blocked, normal OS filesystem cache. Browser times start at navigation with the gateway listening. The constrained profile uses 10 Mbit/s down, 150 ms latency, 4× CPU slowdown. No external model was called.

| Median, seconds | Base | PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| Command → first successful HTTP `/` | 10.35 | 10.09 |
| Desktop: new chat can type / `/help` acknowledged | 0.67 / 2.25 | 0.89 / 3.58 |
| Desktop: existing chat text visible | 2.50 | 1.23 |
| Constrained: bootstrap request starts | 1.01 | 0.40 |
| Constrained: new chat can type / `/help` acknowledged | 1.92 / 3.54 | 1.86 / 3.31 |
| Constrained: existing chat text visible | 3.33 | 3.29 |

The command-to-HTTP ranges overlap: **8.75–10.88 s → 5.78–14.28 s**. Separately timing both recovery scans on three fresh restores per version gave **2.60 → 0.19 s** combined; both versions emitted the same number of recovery events and no inbound work. These stage savings did not translate to equivalent launch savings.

A separate first-open check (three paired process starts; the *only* page opened was desktop new chat) also reproduced the send regression: typing **0.243 → 0.258 s**, server acknowledgement **0.751 → 1.543 s**, with command-to-HTTP **11.71 → 6.65 s**. This separates initial navigation from background work left by a previous chat.

All 40 mixed-scenario browser contexts used one bootstrap and had no unexpected HTTP or page errors. The gateway acknowledged each `/help`; every history page returned the same 172 persisted events. Separately checked visible text against the response and verified that a clean, unauthenticated deep link gets a 401, no socket and no composer. Production build, 535 focused Python tests (one skipped), 31 browser fixture cases, and the corrected live component-gallery coverage case passed locally. The production asset manifest is unchanged by that gallery-only correction. No private content, identifiers or credentials are attached.

Contributes to [NAN-458](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-458).

| Before: login expired, switch incorrectly off | After: same failure, switch on | After turning it off and refreshing |

## Why

Copying a reply on desktop used to take two clicks: open the `…` menu, then choose Copy. The narrow layout already offered one-click copy. Desktop should be just as quick without putting a permanent toolbar in the reading column.

- Remove unused menu attributes and CSS. Replace assertions about DOM nesting and pointer-event styles with browser checks of placement and an actual clipboard read.

Narrow screens and devices without hover keep their existing touch controls. This is a WebUI change only; it does not change gateway behavior, data formats or the client/host contract.

## What changed

Consolidates tests without changing production code, CI selection, coverage thresholds or timeouts. Across 86 test files, 166 old test identifiers were removed or replaced and 10 new identifiers carry grouped or renamed cases: **12,185 → 12,029 static test declarations (−156 net)**. No suite file was removed. On Windows with all channel dependencies installed, actual pytest collection went from **12,240 to 12,109 items (−131)**. Parameterized declarations, loop-generated browser tests, and collected items are different units; this is not a CI speedup claim.

- The CLI `agent -c` journey checks both the selected config path and the path actually loaded, without constructing two fake runtimes. Gateway config and cron routing still have their own entrypoint coverage.
- Provider lookup tests now check canonical lookup and backend metadata together where they asserted the same registry entry. Individual provider routing, credential selection, serialized request fields and failure modes remain separate.
- Dropped the Signal helper's uncallable empty-sender case; the notification entrypoint still exercises its empty-input early return. The QQ and WeCom filename traversal cases look identical but were kept: they guard different implementations.

prs.title: fix(agent): isolate inline command failures
prs.body:
## Problem

  `/status` runs inline in `AgentLoop.run()`, outside the session worker's exception handling. If session loading or runtime resolution raises an unhandled
  exception, it escapes the command handler and terminates the consumer.

  The loop then calls `aclose()`, cancelling active tasks in other sessions and closing shared resources. Under the standard gateway startup path, the runtime task
  failure also triggers gateway cleanup.

  ## Changes

  - Catch ordinary handler exceptions at the inline command execution boundary.
  - Log the failure while respecting the session's logging policy.
  - Reuse `TurnDelivery.fail()` to send a safe error response with the request's routing metadata.
  - Avoid publishing completion or idle events for an already active session.
  - Preserve existing session queue/conflict exception handling and `CancelledError` propagation.

  Successful command dispatch and response publication remain unchanged.

prs.title: feat(webui): edit and resend messages in the same session
prs.body:
**Current head: `a51f1ea21`, based on `main` at `0c45c7441`.** [All 20 CI checks passed](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/45027140708), including `CI required`. The Windows benchmarks and CI run below apply to earlier snapshots, not the current head.

Related to [NAN-92](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-92/webui-支持编辑并重新发送已发送的用户消息).

## What users get

In a saved topic, select **Edit message** beside your message on desktop, or under **Message actions** on mobile, to open an inline draft. **Cancel** preserves the conversation and composer. **Resend** replaces the selected message and its suffix and generates a reply in the same topic. **Fork** still makes a separate topic. This does not undo external tool effects. Edit the text of ordinary messages, including captions on uploads and local file attachments. Resending reuses the original files rather than uploading them again. If a file is missing or access has been revoked, the conversation and draft stay intact. Quotes, mentions, commands and special inputs are not converted to plain text. [User guide](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/blob/a51f1ea21be4420ea50e9728bc64777db8d6bb49/docs/webui.md#edit-a-sent-message).

## Current behavior and verification

Edit-and-resend is an in-place fork at the selected input. A normal fork copies the prefix to a new topic; resend keeps that prefix in the same topic and writes the replacement. Both use the same prefix and transactional persistence code. A later append is not a conflict: resending at B discards an already appended C. A normal message sent after the replacement continues the current topic; it has no history-version precondition. A genuinely missing fork point cannot select a different row. Other connected tabs receive the replacement over WebSocket.

The session transaction stores the replacement and the original attachment references in the existing durable input queue. The worker then handles that input exactly as it handles a normal send. The model loop has no edit/fork branch, and a retry does not generate a second reply. Local file access is checked again before truncating the conversation.

On `25d2bcdbf`, two Chromium tabs on the production-built local gateway verified both message ordering and attachment reuse with a real model. A text file was uploaded once; changing the question made the model retrieve a different value from that same file. The second tab updated without reloading and the file remained attached after refresh. The restart regression also exercises resuming an accepted, not yet executed replacement with an image. Focused Python, UI and browser checks, the production build, type checks and import boundaries passed. Two unrelated startup-language UI tests also fail on the preceding head. The earlier Windows benchmarks were not rerun.

## Earlier verification (`68c11eaf0`)

[Earlier CI](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/44917107465). Synced `main` at `0dc8679ed`. On desktop and a 390px viewport, opening the editor on a collapsed message exposes the full text and resend controls; cancel restores the original collapsed message and keyboard focus. Edit admission no longer decodes answer bodies to identify the discarded suffix. A concurrent SQLite writer test verifies that a history page and its ETag describe the same snapshot and an edit based on an obsolete page is rejected.

### Historical comparison: `0dc8679ed` vs `68c11eaf0`

Both snapshots were separately production-built on Windows and run against the same deterministic loopback model, fixture data, dependencies and browser. Eight fresh gateway pairs × 16 measured pairs per operation; startup and within-pair order were balanced. Differences are PR minus `main`, in ms. For all five shared operations the one-sided 95% upper bound on the paired median was below the existing margin. This measures typical latency on this runner, not every device or tail latency.

| Shared operation | Paired median Δ | One-sided 95% upper bound | Margin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Latest history (8 turns) | -0.29 | +0.61 | 1.00 |
| Latest history (192 turns) | -0.83 | +0.25 | 1.00 |
| Ordinary input acknowledgement | -0.20 | +0.20 | 1.00 |
| Ordinary input → completed reply | -2.44 | +0.56 | 5.00 |
| Navigate → latest message painted | +0.60 | +4.90 | 5.00 |

`main` has no edit-and-resend operation, so it has no like-for-like timing for that new feature. Earlier results against an older integration parent and the previous edit implementation are [historical diagnostics](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-92#comment-59285eab-02f7-45da-bd22-d08700295c79), not the readiness gate. [Measurement plan, all 640 raw pairs and confidence intervals for the current comparison](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-92#comment-03da91ef-d8e0-464f-940a-7719408576c5).

## Correctness evidence on `e42f74689`

- One owner serializes ordinary input and edits. The SQLite transaction checks the page-independent source identity, original text, revision and retry receipt, then changes both model history and display history. Admission failure leaves the old histories intact. Once accepted, a model failure belongs to the new turn. A transport retry does not schedule a second model request.
- **White-box:** reviewed admission/dispatch, cancellation, storage/crash boundaries, outbound ownership, HTTP pagination and frontend draft/connection lifecycle. Fixed canonical `input_id` on replacement and a late idle event that could leave its original run marked active. The late event releases only that owner and does not publish into a replaced history. Final focused Python selection: 81 passed.
- **Black-box:** two Chromium clients, production-built UI, real local gateway/SQLite/WebSocket and a deterministic HTTP model. Mouse, keyboard and touch; cancel with an outstanding composer draft; middle, first and paginated edits; reload and actual disconnect/reconnect. The provider saw exactly 3, 0 and 174 retained user inputs respectively, followed only by the edited input, once per edit. Older retained rows remained pageable; the topic/identity did not change. Two editors of the same revision produced one winner; reconnect/retry, busy/stale source, provider refusal and ordinary fork were checked independently. No uncaught browser exceptions. No physical device or external model was used.
- **Formal concurrency check:** [two TLA+ models, assumptions and reproduction commands](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/tree/e42f74689b0e41915d0c7d52939092cd50f4b062/verification/history-edit). All invariants held over 484 admission states and 132 delayed-delivery/reconnect states, with no unexpected deadlock. Removing transactional source validation or the retired-generation fence gave the expected counterexamples. These are bounded single-owner models assuming atomic SQLite commits, not an exactly-once guarantee for external side effects.

## Historical CI and snapshots (`e42f74689`)

[Test Suite 44722331397](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/44722331397) passed, including `CI required`. PR head `e42f74689`; Actions checked out `5a0fd420d`, merging that head onto `db0306b40`. The local correctness and timing runs use the PR head; ordinary timing uses its frozen integration parent `cd75dbfaa`, not moving main. No check or size/coverage budget was relaxed. Attempt 1's Windows native upgrade/recovery test reached the second `metadata-loss` journey, then `inspect_profiles()` raised `ValueError` while checking readiness after the second restart. The exact target's push CI skipped native acceptance. The preceding PR candidate passed the same step. Only that Windows job and downstream aggregate were re-requested on the unchanged merge; the original failure is not attributed to the edit without evidence. [First attempt's failure report](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/actions/runs/44722331397/artifacts/14624090600).

<details><summary>Historical performance results and diagnosis on e42f74689 (superseded by the current table above)</summary>

### Performance

**At that snapshot, performance was not signed off:** Latest page, 8 turns, Latest page, 192 turns, Ordinary input → completed reply, Navigate → latest message painted, Edit → completed reply. Do not treat passing CI as performance approval.

Windows, real same-version gateway/WebUI with a deterministic loopback model. Ordinary operations vs `cd75dbfaa` (integration parent); edits vs `d06d326ad` (previous edit implementation). Four fresh gateway pairs, 16 measured pairs each, per metric. Snapshots on the same volume. AB/BA balanced at startup and randomized within adjacent pairs; warmups excluded, no other observations discarded. Reads decode eight real HTTP responses per observation. Render requires the expected message in view followed by an animation frame. Edit replaces turn 49 of 96, with one provider execution and the exact retained prefix. All durations are ms.

| Path | Baseline median | PR median | Paired Δ [two-sided 95% interval] | One-sided upper / margin | Gate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Latest page, 8 turns | 13.21 | 14.36 | +0.88 [-0.28, +1.62] | +1.54 / 1.00 | Not established |
| Latest page, 192 turns | 14.70 | 15.27 | +0.64 [-0.51, +1.60] | +1.19 / 1.00 | Not established |
| Ordinary input ACK | 6.07 | 5.85 | +0.05 [-0.38, +0.53] | +0.48 / 1.00 | Pass |
| Ordinary input → completed reply | 70.04 | 72.48 | +1.91 [-1.51, +6.17] | +5.22 / 5.00 | Not established |
| Navigate → latest message painted | 99.65 | 95.45 | -0.15 [-7.80, +7.20] | +5.30 / 5.00 | Not established |
| Edit ACK | 13.19 | 10.79 | -1.57 [-2.25, -0.85] | -0.92 / 1.00 | Pass |
| Edit → completed reply | 86.31 | 100.96 | +9.27 [+3.27, +14.12] | +14.02 / 5.00 | Not established |

The gate is the one-sided 95% upper bound on the paired median delta (candidate minus baseline), strictly below max(5% of the baseline median, 1 ms for reads/ACKs or 5 ms for completed turns/render). Intervals use 12,000 deterministic stratified bootstrap draws across observations within the four blocks. Cross-block and machine-to-machine variability, tails, physical-device latency and the latency of an external model are not bounded by this test.

On the previous `aa18f9e45` snapshot (48 pairs; gateway blocks separated in time), short/long reads had paired medians +1.67/+2.24 ms and upper bounds +2.80/+3.43 ms vs a 1 ms margin. Ordinary ACK, paint and edit completion also failed to establish non-inferiority. Profiling identified a duplicate SQLite snapshot-header lookup. This candidate reuses immutable headers only within one transaction and sends the regular 40-event page after replacement, with a cursor for the rest. The previous samples were retained, not pooled.


| Path | Baseline / candidate block medians (ms), in measurement order | Min–max of all samples: baseline / candidate (ms) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Latest page, 8 turns | 19.14 / 20.84; 11.75 / 14.21; 13.03 / 12.07; 12.95 / 12.93 | 6.92–24.56 / 6.77–26.59 |
| Latest page, 192 turns | 22.50 / 17.84; 13.20 / 14.74; 12.98 / 12.78; 14.03 / 14.99 | 7.40–25.67 / 8.04–26.99 |
| Ordinary input ACK | 5.75 / 6.21; 7.06 / 7.07; 5.77 / 5.41; 5.77 / 5.77 | 4.70–24.72 / 4.66–37.74 |
| Ordinary input → completed reply | 66.80 / 70.06; 84.42 / 92.85; 68.16 / 69.86; 67.26 / 69.63 | 59.76–114.63 / 59.57–130.79 |
| Navigate → latest message painted | 90.60 / 90.45; 102.80 / 108.55; 102.30 / 100.40; 92.70 / 90.90 | 65.50–163.60 / 67.20–149.50 |
| Edit ACK | 11.10 / 10.02; 12.36 / 9.92; 16.95 / 13.63; 13.63 / 12.48 | 10.03–25.28 / 7.71–186.72 |
| Edit → completed reply | 74.88 / 87.17; 78.57 / 82.53; 114.81 / 123.42; 93.31 / 109.56 | 68.64–346.62 / 70.84–463.34 |

Independent tracing found prompt-context observation and four display-history appends on both current main and the candidate, versus two appends on the previous edit implementation. This explains a candidate path to optimize; it does not assign the full end-to-end difference to one function. Recheck the shared delivery path on a quiet runner without dropping context graphs, persistence or generation checks. In ordinary HTTP reads the candidate already makes fewer SQL statements (25/37 vs 27/39), selects the same 24/42 records, and does not load full model history. prs.title: fix(mcp): isolate server startup and retries from chat
prs.body:
## Summary

A slow or unresponsive MCP server no longer blocks ordinary chat or delays tools from healthy servers. The gateway reports slow startup after 10 seconds and cancels an unfinished startup attempt after 60 seconds. Tools that become ready during a turn are available on the next model request. Users do not need to send another message to use them.

This is a draft for design review. The change is not ready to merge.

## Benchmarks

### Latest change: use a tool that becomes ready mid-turn

A real gateway and stdio MCP server processed one user message against a local test model endpoint. The first request arrived before the MCP server was ready. The server finished discovery during that request, and the model made a built-in tool call to continue the same turn. We did not send a follow-up message.

| What we measured | Better result | Previous draft `2065ef90f1` | Current draft `bc62a8a82` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First chat request reaches the model endpoint | Lower; one paired run, not a latency comparison at scale | 1.22 s | 1.25 s |
| Model can call the newly ready MCP tool | Earlier, with a successful tool result | Not available during the current turn | Available on request 2; request 3 received `pong` |
| Ordered definitions on consecutive requests with no further tool change | Identical | Identical where the list was unchanged | Identical on requests 2 and 3; existing definitions stayed in their original order |

The tool list can change when a tool becomes ready. A model provider may reuse less of the previous prompt on that request. The earlier equal-prefix result does not apply to this transition. No provider cache hit rate was measured.

### Previous change: slow startup, timeout, and chat

**Compare:** draft `47edc783fa` vs. draft `2065ef90f1`. Both ran the same gateway workload on macOS arm64 with Python 3.11, real stdio MCP child processes, and a local model endpoint. The endpoint captures model requests and returns test responses. No external model was called.

**Result:** Chat latency was similar in these runs, and the reusable prompt prefix did not change. The slow server still worked. The unresponsive child exited, and the next attempts started after the expected delays.

| What we measured | Better result | `47edc783fa` | `2065ef90f1` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **First chat request reaches the model endpoint** with a 12-second MCP startup in the background. Time starts when the client sends the chat message. | **Lower** | 1.14–1.17 s | 1.06–1.21 s |
| **Slow MCP tool becomes available** with the same 12-second startup. Time starts when the gateway process launches. The tool must return `pong`. | **Lower**, with a successful tool call | 13.41–13.75 s; `pong` | 13.33–13.40 s; `pong` |
| **A child that never answers the handshake exits** while the gateway stays running. Time starts when the gateway process launches. | **Lower**; no child left running after cleanup | Still alive after 63 s; no startup deadline | Exited and reported a timeout at 62.86–63.12 s |
| **Wait before restarting an unresponsive child**, measured from timeout cleanup to the next child launch. | **Match the target**, not faster: 15 s, then 30 s | No retry; the original attempt was still running | 15.12 s, then 30.16 s; no overlapping child processes |
| **Reusable prompt prefix** across two model requests for one user input. The MCP tool becomes ready between the requests. | **Higher** for the same workload; **unchanged** is the goal for this timeout change | 5,259 identical tokens | 5,259 identical tokens; same prefix content |

The first two rows show the range of two paired runs. The chat measurement includes gateway and network overhead; the **1-second** limit applies only to how long the gateway waits for initial MCP discovery. The **10-second** slow notice does not cancel the process. The **60-second** deadline starts cancellation; the timeout is visible after transport cleanup. A healthy sibling tool returned `pong` before and after that timeout.

The cache row counts tokens in the **matching start of two requests**, not extra tokens sent or billed. We normalized temporary checkout and workspace paths and used the same tokenizer on both sides. Ordered tool definitions matched byte for byte across all four compared requests. The next user input called the recovered tool. These measurements do **not** show a live provider's cache hit rate.

<details>
<summary>Earlier benchmarks: discovery, reconnect, and the tool list</summary>

These measurements use different earlier versions or prototypes. Each row identifies its comparison; they are not all comparisons with `main` or new runs on the latest commit. The original PR base was `d3bb330f57`.

| What we measured | Better result | Reference | Earlier PR result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First chat request reaches the model endpoint while a 12-second MCP server starts | **Lower** | Original `main`: 12.64 s | 1.11–1.13 s |
| Healthy MCP tool becomes available next to an unresponsive peer, using the slower configuration order in two runs | **Lower** | Serial background prototype: 2.91–3.17 s | Per-server discovery: 0.43–0.52 s |
| A 12-second stdio MCP tool becomes available after the gateway launches | **Lower**, with a successful tool call | Draft `f02258e39e`: no tool within 16 s | 13.2–13.7 s; returned `pong` |
| Healthy MCP tool becomes available when four unresponsive servers are configured ahead of it | **Lower** | Draft `f02258e39e`: 11.6–11.7 s | 2.45–2.58 s |
| Hot reload replaces a stalled server: time to a successful tool call | **Lower** | Draft `f02258e39e`: 10.05 s | 0.23 s |
| A healthy server reconnects while another server stalls: time to a successful tool call | **Lower** | Draft `f02258e39e`: 10.01 s | 0.22 s |
| Status requests in 60 seconds while Apps is open and a server is still connecting | **Lower** if Apps still shows the result | Old polling schedule: 61 | 21; same schedule for the first 10 s |
| Reusable prefix with a tool added between two requests in the same turn | **Higher** for the same workload | Live tool list: 4,360 matching tokens | Tool list held for the turn: 5,305 matching tokens |
| Total input tokens in request 1 / request 2 in that same cache test | **Lower** if the requests still support the same task | Live tool list: 5,306 / 5,462 | Tool list held for the turn: 5,305 / 5,423 |
| Discovery time for 4,000 synthetic tool definitions through the connector, with no network | **Lower** | Draft `0c367b5a2d`: 36.48 ms | 28.87 ms; same ordered tool definitions |
| Discovery time with an allowlist that selects 40 of the 4,000 definitions | **Lower** | Draft `0c367b5a2d`: 12.85 ms | 6.72 ms; same result |

The healthy-peer test used the same 2.5-second test timeout on both sides. It measures when a tool becomes available, not when a model answers. The reload and reconnect rows are single paired observations. The Apps row uses a virtual clock. The synthetic discovery values are medians of three interleaved batches, not end-to-end latency. The token rows are local estimates, not provider usage or cache hit rate.

</details>

### Verification

- Recovery follow-up (`3022ed495`): cancelling a tool call while its old connection closes no longer stops background recovery. Reload and shutdown drain that cleanup before proceeding. Apps continues polling after ordinary connection failures and reflects recovery without a page refresh.
- This follow-up passed 392 focused Python tests (one Windows-only case skipped on Linux), 20 WebUI component tests, WebUI type checking/build, focused lint, and the Python import-boundary check. A real HTTP MCP fixture verified cancellation, recovery, reload, and shutdown. A real Chromium browser against the built WebUI and an isolated gateway showed a failed stdio MCP recover without refreshing the page. All test MCP children exited. The full CI and native upgrade matrices were not rerun locally.
- The `bc62a8a82` draft passed 266 focused Python tests, the import-boundary check, and Ruff. In a separate real gateway run, a healthy MCP tool returned `pong` while its peer was stalled. A peer configured to delay startup by 12 seconds later connected and returned `pong`. No test MCP child remained after shutdown.

- A real Chromium browser used the authenticated Gateway and the built Apps page. It showed slow startup, recovery, and timeout, and exposed **Reconnect** for the timed-out server.
- The preceding draft passed **403 Python tests**, **347 Python tests with minimum dependencies**, and **19 WebUI tests**. The Python checks cover transport cleanup, hot reload, request formatting, proxy and redirect safeguards, and protected gateway activation. WebUI type checking and build, import boundary checks, and Ruff also passed.
- Earlier real stdio checks verified that a name conflict could not send a tool call to the wrong server. Renaming and reloading restored the tool under the new name. The timeout follow-up did not re-run the full native packaged-upgrade matrix.

## Before this PR

The gateway waits for MCP connection attempts before it starts the agent. Its readiness hook also waits for another attempt before each turn. A configured MCP process that starts but never replies can delay ordinary chat, even when the user does not need an MCP tool. If a process fails quickly, the next message can start it again. Serial discovery also delays other MCP servers.

Keeping chat off the connection path also lets a server finish discovery during a turn. The next model request uses the live tool list. An earlier draft held additions until the next user input to preserve a longer prompt prefix, but that could hide a useful tool for the rest of a long turn.

## How the draft works

1. **Gateway and MCP lifecycle.** The gateway starts one MCP maintenance task after normal startup admission. It gives initial discovery one shared window of up to one second. It does not wait for MCP in each chat, Dream, or heartbeat run. The provider cancels an unfinished startup attempt after 60 seconds and closes its transport before retrying. Failed attempts retry independently of chat after 15, 30, 60, then at most 120 seconds. The delay resets after a successful connection or a configuration change.
2. **Separate discovery from publication.** The connector opens one server and returns one handle for its capabilities and cleanup. It does not write to a tool registry. The provider permits up to four concurrent stdio process launches. The handshake and discovery do not hold a launch slot or the configuration lock. Each configured server has at most one connection attempt, so stalled servers do not delay healthy ones. A failed server does not publish partial tools. OAuth and the WebUI connection test consume the discovery result directly and keep their own deadlines. Each SDK transport still opens and closes in its owning task.
3. **Use live tool definitions during a turn.** Discovery publishes ready tools immediately. The next model request can use them, even for the same user input. Removed tools stop appearing in the next request, and execution still checks the live registry. Built-in tools stay first, and the order stays deterministic when the registry is unchanged. This change does not alter an in-flight model request or trigger an extra one.
4. **Do not redirect a conflicting tool name.** Two server names can generate the same wrapped tool name. The provider removes the ambiguous name rather than replacing its target. It unregisters each tool by object ownership, not a name prefix. An ambiguous name cannot be reassigned during the gateway's lifetime. Non-conflicting names stay unchanged. Rename one server or tool and reload to use its new name.
5. **Report the active connection.** The provider uses the active connection and attempt tables for status. Reload revokes removed or changed connections and cancels obsolete attempts. It can return a pending result while discovery continues, instead of canceling a healthy slow connection. The gateway reports a slow connection after ten seconds without canceling it. The Apps page checks every second during the first ten polls, then every five seconds while open and visible. It continues to check after startup times out or a connection fails so it can show the next attempt.

The gateway owns startup and shutdown. The connector owns the SDK connection and discovery. `MCPProvider` owns routing, publication, and retries. The existing runner reads the live tool list for each request. `AgentLoop`, `AgentRunner`, provider payload formats, OAuth consent, network policy, and rules for replaying tool operations do not change. No new installed dependency, setting, or on-disk cache is added. At `bc62a8a82`, the production diff was **+516 / −641** Python lines and **+61 / −17** WebUI lines against the draft base; test and documentation changes are separate.

### Reuse existing libraries

- The existing `referencing` library resolves JSON Pointers inside the document. nanobot still moves local targets under `$defs` for model compatibility. Resolution does not retrieve files or URLs.
- AnyIO provides stream iteration and context-manager cleanup. A small receive adapter keeps malformed progress notifications out of SDK logs, which can otherwise include the raw payload.
- Tools, resources, and prompts use one loop over the MCP SDK's page requests. The loop checks repeated cursors and completes a list before publishing it. The SDK's session group does not fetch subsequent pages, so this change does not use it for discovery.
- SSE and Streamable HTTP use the same preflight and HTTPX client setup for URL validation, proxy routing and redirects. Each transport keeps its own request headers, timeout settings, and SDK lifecycle.
- Tool results use SDK content types directly. Images and embedded image blobs still become local artifacts. Python's stable list sort preserves the exact built-ins-first tool order without maintaining two intermediate lists.
- Discovery reuses each wrapped tool name for the allowlist, diagnostics, and registration. The allowlist still runs before tool schemas are normalized. The turn-history owner preserves MCP mention metadata directly; its unused WebUI import shim is removed.

## Compatibility and open decisions

- **Background discovery:** The ten-second reload wait limits the response, not the lifetime of discovery. A slow stdio handshake can finish after the reload returns, without changing `toolTimeout`. A startup attempt still running at 60 seconds is canceled. The gateway waits for the connection owner to close its transport, even if shutdown overlaps the timeout. A server that really needs more than 60 seconds to start now times out. Interactive OAuth and explicit connection tests retain their own deadlines.
- **Intentional change for conflicting names:** Older versions could silently replace a tool with another tool under the same name. The draft disables that name instead. The configuration guide explains how to rename and reload. Restart the gateway after removing a conflict if you need to restore the original name. This does not change stored configuration or existing non-conflicting names.
- **Update continuity:** An earlier macOS arm64 run used the published 0.4.1 native wheel and the actual 0.4.1 updater code with an isolated local feed. It completed both jumps to private `0.4.2.dev0` and `0.4.2.dev1` fixtures from this source. In a separate run, an injected restart failure restored 0.4.1, and the restored installation then updated successfully to `0.4.2.dev1`. An MCP process started but never replied on the candidate gateways. Existing chat history, later writes, restart, the next update, and the shutdown of all fixture MCP children passed. This is not public-feed, signature, or all-platform upgrade evidence. No settings schema, stored chat data, install layout, or update protocol changes.

## Related work

This builds on the existing MCP lifecycle owner and readiness recovery from #5343 and #5535. It preserves the transport cleanup ownership addressed by #3640 and the tool replay safeguards from #6537.

Resolves [NAN-450](https://linear.app/nanobot-ai/issue/NAN-450/mcp-后台连接不阻塞聊天工具就绪后可在当前轮使用).

prs.title: fix(channels): deliver provider retry waits through an opt-in hook
prs.body:
Fixes #5585

## Problem
When a provider call backs off, core publishes `RetryWaitEvent` ("Model request failed, retry in {n}s (attempt {k}).") but `ChannelManager._dispatch_outbound_loop` dropped it unconditionally, before any channel hook and outside the `sendProgress` gate. Only the interactive CLI ever rendered it, so chat channels looked hung for the whole backoff.

## Change
I went with the less intrusive option from the issue: a default no-op `BaseChannel.send_retry_wait(...)` hook, following the same pattern as `send_delta` / `send_reasoning*`.
- `ChannelManager` now forwards `RetryWaitEvent` to `send_retry_wait` and never falls through to `send()`. Channels that don't override the hook stay silent, so there's no new config key and no extra chat messages by default.
- I didn't route it through `sendProgress`: that defaults to on, so every progress-enabled channel would get a permanent chat line. This matches the precedent in #5799 (compaction notices).
- Linear already built an ephemeral thought for this event inside `send()`, but that code was unreachable because of the drop. It now lives in `LinearChannel.send_retry_wait`, and `send()` delegates to it, so direct sends behave the same.
- WebSocket/WebUI is unchanged (it uses the structured `RetryStatusEvent`).
- `docs/channel-package-guide.md` documents the hook.

## Tests
- New `tests/channels/test_channel_manager_retry_wait.py` covers two cases: a channel that implements the hook receives the notice even with `send_progress` false, and default channels don't get it through `send()`. The hook test failed before the fix.
- A Linear test covers the ephemeral thought and direct `send()` delegation.

## Verification (Linux, Python 3.11, GH tokens unset)
- `uv sync --all-extras --dev`, channel dependency install, `uv pip check`: exit 0
- `uv run --no-sync ruff check nanobot tests conftest.py`: exit 0
- `uv run --no-sync basedpyright`: exit 0 (0 errors)
- `uv run --no-sync python -m pytest -n 2 --dist loadfile --ignore=tests/cli/test_commands.py`: exit 0 (9220 passed, 48 skipped)
- `uv run --no-sync python -m pytest tests/cli/test_commands.py`: exit 0 (160 passed)
- Not run locally: the Python 3.14 coverage cell, Windows, and Docker.

This change was prepared with help from an AI coding assistant and reviewed by me.

prs.title: [security] fix(mcp): prevent enabledTools name collisions
prs.body:
## Summary
This PR hardens the MCP `enabledTools` capability boundary so lossy sanitized wrapped names cannot authorize a different raw MCP tool.

- Fixes a model-visible MCP tool identity confusion path where raw names such as `demo.read`, `demo/read`, `demo read`, and `demo__read` normalize to the same wrapped name.
- Keeps exact raw MCP tool names as the unambiguous allowlist identity for lossy names.
- Preserves wrapped-name compatibility for stable names that do not change during sanitization.
- Adds focused regression coverage and a Docker stdio-MCP proof that the previous colliding wrapped-name path now registers no tool.

## Security issues covered

| Issue | Impact | Severity |
|-------|--------|----------|
| MCP `enabledTools` wrapped-name collision | A mutable or malicious MCP server could cause an unapproved raw tool to inherit approval from a colliding model-visible wrapped name. In credential-bearing MCP deployments, this can bypass the operator's intended least-privilege tool boundary. | Medium; potentially higher in credential-bearing/action-bearing MCP deployments |

## Before this PR
- `enabledTools` accepted either raw MCP tool names or sanitized wrapped names such as `mcp_test_demo_read`.
- The wrapped names were generated through `_sanitize_name(...)`, which is lossy and many-to-one.
- A raw tool named `demo/read` could be registered when the operator allowlisted only `mcp_test_demo_read`, even though that wrapped name could have been produced by a different raw tool such as `demo.read`.
- Ambiguous wrapped names could also collide when all MCP tools were enabled, risking duplicate model-visible tool identities.

## After this PR
- Exact raw MCP names remain supported as the precise allowlist identity.
- Wrapped-name `enabledTools` entries only match when the wrapped name is stable and does not depend on lossy sanitization.
- Ambiguous wrapped-name groups are detected before registration.
- Ambiguous tools are skipped when all tools are enabled so duplicate model-visible MCP names do not silently overwrite each other.
- Regression tests lock in rejection for sanitized wrapped-name authorization and ambiguous wrapped-name groups.

## Why this matters
`enabledTools` is a least-privilege boundary for model-callable MCP tools. When that boundary uses lossy generated names as identities, a tool with a different raw MCP name can be registered under an approved model-visible name.

This matters most for MCP servers that carry credentials or side effects, such as repository, API, browser, database, or cloud integrations. A compromised, malicious, or mutable MCP endpoint should not be able to change raw tool names and inherit an operator's prior approval for a different capability.

## How this differs from related issue/PR
This is adjacent to the merged MCP `enabledTools` fix in [#4436](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/pull/4436), `fix(tools): gate MCP resource and prompt registration behind enabledTools`, which merged on 2026-06-25 and fixed [#4435](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/issues/4435).

| Merged PR | Boundary covered | What it fixed | Why this PR is still needed |
|-----------|------------------|---------------|-----------------------------|
| [#4436](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/pull/4436) | MCP resource/prompt registration under `enabledTools` | When a server used `enabledTools: []` or a specific tool list, ordinary tools were filtered but MCP resources and prompts were still registered and exposed. #4436 now registers resources/prompts only when the server is effectively allow-all (`["*"]`). | #4436 did not change the identity used for ordinary MCP tool allowlisting. A raw tool can still be authorized through a lossy sanitized wrapped name unless the tool-name boundary is hardened. |
| This PR | MCP ordinary tool identity under `enabledTools` | A wrapped/model-visible name such as `mcp_test_demo_read` could authorize a different raw MCP tool such as `demo/read` because `_sanitize_name(...)` is many-to-one. | It closes the sibling tool-identity path so `enabledTools` cannot be bypassed by raw-name collisions after resources/prompts are already gated. |

In short:
- [#4436](https://github.com/HKUDS/nanobot/pull/4436) made `enabledTools` apply consistently across MCP capability *types* by blocking resources/prompts whenever the operator configured a restricted tool set.
- This PR makes `enabledTools` apply safely within the ordinary MCP *tool* type by ensuring an approved wrapped name cannot identify multiple or lossy raw MCP tool names.
- The vulnerable code path here is the tool registration allowlist check in `connect_mcp_servers(...)`, not the resource/prompt registration path fixed by #4436.
- Both fixes are needed because they protect adjacent layers of the same MCP least-privilege boundary: capability type coverage first, then capability identity correctness.

## Attack flow
```text
Operator allowlists a wrapped MCP tool name such as mcp_test_demo_read
    -> MCP server advertises a different raw tool such as demo/read
        -> Nanobot sanitizes the raw name to the same wrapped name
            -> enabledTools wrapped-name check treats it as approved
                -> the model-visible tool calls the unapproved raw MCP capability
```

## Affected code

| Issue | Files |
|-------|-------|
| MCP wrapped-name identity collision | `nanobot/agent/tools/mcp.py`, `tests/tools/test_mcp_tool.py` |

## Root cause
Issue 1: MCP `enabledTools` wrapped-name collision
- `_sanitize_name(...)` intentionally converts provider-incompatible characters to underscores and collapses runs.
- The result is not a stable authorization identity because multiple raw names can map to the same wrapped name.
- `connect_mcp_servers(...)` previously accepted the wrapped name directly in `enabledTools` without proving that it uniquely and reversibly identified the raw MCP tool.

## CVSS assessment

| Issue | CVSS v3.1 | Vector |
|-------|-----------|--------|
| MCP `enabledTools` wrapped-name collision | 4.2 Medium | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N` |

Rationale:
- The attacker condition is a malicious, compromised, or mutable configured MCP server, or an actor able to influence that server's advertised tool list.
- The direct bug is a capability-boundary bypass, not default unauthenticated code execution.
- Impact can be higher in deployments where the affected MCP server has credential-bearing or action-bearing tools, but this PR keeps the universal claim bounded to the authorization boundary failure.

## Safe reproduction steps
1. Configure an MCP server named `test` with `enabledTools: ["mcp_test_demo_read"]`.
2. Have that MCP server advertise only the raw tool name `demo/read`.
3. On vulnerable code, connect the MCP server and inspect the registered tool.
4. Observe that `mcp_test_demo_read` is registered even though the backing raw name is `demo/read`.
5. Execute `mcp_test_demo_read` and observe the raw MCP call goes to `demo/read`.

## Expected vulnerable behavior
On vulnerable code, the Docker stdio-MCP proof showed:

```text
enabledTools= ['mcp_test_demo_read']
registered_tool_names= ['mcp_test_demo_read']
registered_original_name= demo/read
execute_result= COLLIDING_TOOL_EXECUTED
expected_unapproved_raw_name= demo/read
```

After this PR, the same safe proof registers no tool:

```text
enabledTools= ['mcp_test_demo_read']
registered_tool_names= []
collision_blocked= true
```

## Changes in this PR
- Builds a wrapped-name to raw-name map before applying `enabledTools`.
- Detects ambiguous wrapped names generated by lossy sanitization.
- Allows wrapped-name matching only when the wrapped name is stable and unambiguous.
- Requires exact raw-name allowlisting for raw MCP names that need lossy sanitization.
- Skips ambiguous wrapped-name groups under wildcard allow-all to avoid duplicate model-visible registrations.
- Adds tests for sanitized wrapped-name rejection, ambiguous wrapped-name rejection, wildcard ambiguity handling, and exact raw-name compatibility.

## Files changed

| Category | Files | What changed |
|----------|-------|--------------|
| MCP registration hardening | `nanobot/agent/tools/mcp.py` | Tightens `enabledTools` matching around raw names, wrapped names, and ambiguous sanitized names. |
| Regression tests | `tests/tools/test_mcp_tool.py` | Adds focused tests for lossy wrapped-name rejection and collision handling. |

## Maintainer impact
- Existing exact raw-name `enabledTools` entries continue to work.
- Existing wrapped-name entries for stable tool names such as `demo` continue to work.
- Wrapped-name entries for raw MCP names that require sanitization now fail closed and should be changed to the exact raw MCP tool name.
- Ambiguous MCP tool name groups are skipped rather than silently producing duplicate model-visible identities.

## Fix rationale
The raw MCP tool name is the only precise identity available from the server. A sanitized model-visible wrapper is useful for provider compatibility, but it is not safe as an authorization identity when sanitization changes the name or when multiple raw names normalize to the same wrapper.

Failing closed in those cases preserves least privilege and makes unsafe configuration visible through warnings instead of silently registering the wrong capability.

## Type of change
- [x] Security hardening / bug fix
- [x] Regression tests
- [ ] Documentation-only change
- [ ] Refactor with no behavior change

## Test plan
The following commands were run successfully:

```bash
uv run --extra dev python -m pytest tests/tools/test_mcp_tool.py -q
# 68 passed
```

```bash
uv run --extra dev python -m ruff check nanobot/agent/tools/mcp.py tests/tools/test_mcp_tool.py
# All checks passed
```

```bash
git diff --check
# passed with no output
```

Docker stdio-MCP fixed-behavior proof:

```bash
docker run --rm \
  -v /path/to/nanobot:/repo \
  -v /path/to/mcp_collision_server.py:/tmp/mcp_collision_server.py:ro \
  -v /path/to/repro_mcp_enabledtools_collision_fixed.py:/tmp/repro_mcp_enabledtools_collision_fixed.py:ro \
  -w /repo \
  ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.12-bookworm-slim \
  uv run --extra dev python /tmp/repro_mcp_enabledtools_collision_fixed.py
# registered_tool_names= []
# collision_blocked= true
```

Docker focused test run:

  uv run --extra dev python -m pytest tests/tools/test_mcp_tool.py -q

## Disclosure notes
This PR is intentionally bounded to MCP `enabledTools` identity handling. It does not claim default unauthenticated takeover, arbitrary host file read, secret theft, or RCE. The impact is an MCP capability-boundary bypass that becomes more serious when the configured MCP server has credential-bearing or action-bearing tools.

issues.title: Autostart scheduled task spawns an elevated gateway despite RunLevel=LeastPrivilege on built-in-Administrator machines - gateway_elevated lockout recurs on every reboot (path not covered by 08bd8a24)
issues.body:
## Environment

- Windows 10 build 19045, hermes-agent v0.23.3 (local checkout `caafe5389`, includes `08bd8a24`)
- Account: built-in Administrator (RID-500). UAC: `EnableLUA=1`, `FilterAdministratorToken=1`, `ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=0`
- Autostart: installer-created task `\Hermes_Gateway` — LogonTrigger (+30 s delay), principal `Administrator` / `InteractiveToken` / `RunLevel=LeastPrivilege`, action `wscript.exe //B //Nologo "...\gateway-service\Hermes_Gateway.vbs"`

## Summary

On this machine the Task Scheduler hands an **elevated** token to a task registered as `LeastPrivilege` under the built-in Administrator's `InteractiveToken` principal. Consequently, on every reboot the autostart task spawns an **elevated gateway**, and any non-elevated desktop app is then permanently locked out with `gateway_elevated` — the same symptom as #154383, but through a different spawn path: the gateway is spawned by the task engine -> `wscript` -> `python`, never going through `spawn_unmanaged_gateway`, so the `client_elevated` guard from 08bd8a24 cannot see it.

Everything else on the machine filters correctly: `explorer.exe`, the desktop app and all shell-launched processes run non-elevated under the same interactive logon (token-inspected). Only the task-engine token comes out elevated.

## Evidence

**1. Real lockout (2026-11-19, pre-fix build — but the task path is unaffected by the client-side fix):**

- Reboot 17:59:56 local; logon task fires (+30 s)
- Gateway PID 23952 started 18:02:09; `OpenProcessToken` + `GetTokenInformation(TokenElevation)` -> **ELEVATED=True**; matching `gateway.start` record in `gateway-exit-diag.log`
- Desktop app was not running at that time; no other launcher in play
- Non-elevated desktop instances launched afterwards were rejected with `gateway_elevated` until the gateway was killed externally and relaunched non-elevated (2026-11-23)

**2. Controlled probe (2026-11-24, on the fixed build):**

Registered a throwaway task whose `Principals` block is byte-identical to `Hermes_Gateway` (`Administrator` / `InteractiveToken` / `RunLevel=LeastPrivilege`), with an action that reports its own token elevation, then `Start-ScheduledTask`:

```
PROBE PID=53040 ELEVATED=True
SESSION=1
INTEGRITY_SID: S-1-16-12288 (High Mandatory Level)
PARENT=svchost.exe (task engine)
```

`LastTaskResult=0`. Probe task removed afterwards. So even on the fixed build, with explicit `LeastPrivilege`, the task engine token is elevated for the built-in Administrator. Registry cross-check at test time: `FilterAdministratorToken=0x1`, `EnableLUA=0x1`, `ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin=0x0`.

## Why the 08bd8a24 guard does not cover this

`spawn_unmanaged_gateway` refuses elevated *clients* asking it to spawn a gateway. The autostart path has no client: task engine -> `wscript.exe` -> `python -m hermes_cli.main gateway run`. Once that elevated gateway runs, the desktop correctly refuses it (per #154383), but nothing prevents the elevated instance from being created at every logon.

## Suggestions

1. Do not rely on the task-engine token for autostart on Windows: e.g. have the task action delegate to the running shell (`explorer.exe "<vbs>"`), which reliably de-elevates. Verified on this machine: from an **elevated** task context, launching the VBS via `explorer.exe` yields a gateway with `ELEVATED=False` (used during our 2026-11-23 recovery).
2. Or have the gateway/VBS check its own token elevation at startup and re-spawn de-elevated (or exit with a clear event-log entry) when it detects an elevated split-token interactive session.
3. Or detect this at install / `hermes doctor` time when registering the task under a RID-500 account and warn.
4. Docs: note that on the built-in Administrator account, task `RunLevel=LeastPrivilege` does not guarantee a filtered token.

Cross-ref: #154383 (client-spawn path, fixed by 08bd8a24). This issue is about the autostart/task-engine path, which remains open.

issues.title: [Bug]: cron run in the hermes console silently resumes a paused job, while the CLI, /cron run and the agent tool refuse

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: comp/cron
labels.description: Cron scheduler and job management

labels.name: tool/file
labels.description: File tools (read, write, patch, search)

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

issues.body:
> [!NOTE]
> 🤖 **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Pi) responding on behalf of @domenicomassafra**

### Bug Description

`cron run <job>` typed in the `hermes console` REPL calls `cron.jobs.trigger_job`, which unconditionally rewrites the job record to `enabled: true` / `state: scheduled` / `paused_at: null` / `paused_reason: null`. A paused or disabled job therefore becomes an active, scheduled job as a side effect of a manual run, and the recorded pause reason is lost.

Every other surface refuses that same request, so one command name has two opposite outcomes:

| Surface | `run` on a paused job |
|---|---|
| `hermes cron run <id>` (CLI) | refused: "Job is paused/disabled; resume it before running." |
| `/cron run <id>` (gateway chat) | refused, prints `cron.did_not_run` with that reason |
| `cronjob(action="run")` (agent tool) | refused, same reason |
| `cron run <id>` (`hermes console`) | resumed, runs, `paused_reason` cleared |

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a job and pause it with a reason: `hermes cron pause <id> --reason "paused by owner"`.
2. `hermes cron run <id>` → prints `Job is paused/disabled; resume it before running.`; the job stays paused. (Correct.)
3. `hermes console`, then `cron run <id>` → prints `Triggered job: <name> [scheduled]`.
4. `hermes cron list` (or the job in `<profile>/cron/jobs.json`).

### Expected Behavior

The console command behaves like the CLI, the agent tool and `/cron run`: a paused or disabled job is not run, or it is run without touching `enabled` / `state` / `paused_at` / `paused_reason`. Resuming stays an explicit `hermes cron resume <id>` / `cron resume <id>`.

If resume-on-manual-run is intended, it should be the same on every surface and documented as such in the `cron run` docs (today the console's own help text says only "Run a job on the next scheduler tick.").

### Actual Behavior

Job record before and after `cron run <id>` inside `hermes console`:

```
BEFORE {'enabled': False, 'state': 'paused', 'paused_at': '…', 'paused_reason': 'paused by owner', 'next_run_at': '…'}
AFTER  {'enabled': True, 'state': 'scheduled', 'paused_at': None, 'paused_reason': None,
        'next_run_at': '<now>', 'manual_run_at': '<now>'}
```

A job that is only disabled (`enabled: false`, `state: scheduled`, no pause) is re-enabled the same way.

### Root Cause Analysis

- `hermes_cli/console_engine.py:789-791` — the console's `_cron_run` handler imports and calls `cron.jobs.trigger_job` directly instead of the shared run path.
- `cron/jobs.py:2227` (`trigger_job`) → writes at `cron/jobs.py:2241-2244`: `enabled: True`, `state: "scheduled"`, `paused_at: None`, `paused_reason: None`. The only guard is `is_terminal_job()` (completed/failed one-shots); paused and disabled jobs are accepted and silently reactivated.
- The refusing surfaces: `tools/cronjob_tools.py:239-252` (`_claim_for_manual_run` → `claim_job_for_fire(manual=True)`, which keeps the paused/disabled gate) and `tools/cronjob_tools.py:181-182` ("keep the normal paused refusal; `trigger_job` would resume the job"). `hermes_cli/cli_cron_lines.py:_job_action_lines` (the gateway `/cron run`) goes through the same tool.
- Resume-on-fire is documented for exactly one caller, `cron/jobs.py:2730` — `claim_job_for_fire(force=True)` = "explicit manual fire, which also resumes the job atomically", i.e. the dashboard's Trigger-now. `trigger_job` documents no resume at all.

On `main` today the same call chain is at `hermes_cli/console_engine.py:790-791`, `cron/jobs.py:2194` (write block `2208-2211`), `tools/cronjob_tools.py:182` and `:249`.

### Proposed Fix

Pick one and make every surface agree:

1. Give `trigger_job` the runnable gate and have the console dispatch through the CLI's path (`cronjob(action="run")` / `_execute_job_now`), so `cron run` refuses paused/disabled jobs exactly like `hermes cron run`; or
2. Keep `trigger_job`'s current behaviour but add an explicit `resume=False` parameter that only the Trigger-now call site sets, so a run never clears `paused_at` / `paused_reason` by accident.

Either way, `paused_reason` should never be dropped by a manual run — it is the audit trail for why a job was stopped.

### Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.23.1 (`3b42157858`), install method git, latest stable release; the same code is on `main` at `36706d42ac`.
- Linux (Ubuntu), Python 3.14.9.
- Affected component: CLI (`hermes console` / `hermes_cli/`), cron scheduler (`cron/jobs.py`).

The Debug Report is intentionally omitted: `hermes debug share` uploads system info, config and logs from a private machine. Everything needed to reproduce is in the steps above; the repro was done on a throwaway `HERMES_HOME` with a single paused job.

issues.body:
## Summary

Since v0.20.0 ("The Herald Release", 2026.8.3) on macOS desktop, Hermes shows two related problems that seem to compound under system load:

1. **Severe resource usage** — the desktop app (renderer + helpers + CLI) continuously consumes >90% CPU combined; renderer has spiked to ~400% CPU. On a Mac Mini M1 (16 GB) this drives system load to ~7.0 and leaves almost no free memory.
2. **Cross-session message routing under load** — messages that belong to other parallel sessions (and automated "You receive the transcript…" style injections that arrive in bursts after external task runs) land inside an *existing active session* instead of a new one. The user sees conversations mixing together chaotically, and the agent ends up executing tasks that were never issued by the user in that session (deploys, config changes, long-running harvests).

The user reports this reproduces more often when multiple sessions run concurrently and the Mac is heavily loaded — and that it only started with the 2.0 update.

## Environment

- Hermes v0.20.0 (git-installed, Xreative fork, updated 2026-08-03)
- macOS desktop app (Hermes.app, Electron)
- Mac Mini M1, 16 GB RAM
- Multiple parallel desktop sessions; cron jobs (some `no_agent` script-only) running every few minutes

## Observed symptoms (measured)

- `ps aux` during incident: Hermes renderer ~40% CPU / 630 MB RSS, helper ~26%, CLI python ~23% — combined >90% continuously.
- Renderer peaks to ~400% CPU have been observed previously (pre-existing note).
- `uptime`: load average 7.04 on an 8-core machine.
- `vm_stat`: only ~75 MB free memory.
- The injected messages are not distinguishable from genuine user messages (same `role=user`), so the agent cannot tell them apart — it acted on them.

## Root-cause hypothesis

- A producer (bursts after external agent task runs) writes "You receive the transcript…" messages into the session store. Under load, these end up appended to the currently active session instead of a fresh session.
- The cleanup cron (`claude-transcript-executor.py`, every 5 min) only selects sessions that have **no assistant output** (`NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM messages WHERE role='assistant')`). As soon as the agent replies to an injected message, the polluted session is no longer detectable and is never cleaned up.

## Expected behavior / suggestions

- Session isolation must be guaranteed: messages from non-user producers should always open a new session (or be explicitly marked, e.g. a distinct `role`/`source` field) so agents can distinguish them from real user input.
- Investigate the desktop renderer CPU/memory leak introduced in 2.0.
- Extend the transcript cleanup watchdog to also flag transcript-marker messages inside sessions that already have assistant output.

Happy to provide logs or reproduce with more detail on request.

labels.name: tool/web

issues.body:
### Problem or Use Case

Version 0.2.0 of the [Agent Skills discovery RFC](https://github.com/cloudflare/agent-skills-discovery-rfc#v020) changed the index:
- **New path:** it lives at `/.well-known/agent-skills/index.json`.
- **Version marker:** it declares `"$schema": "https://schemas.agentskills.io/discovery/0.2.0/schema.json"`.
- **New skill entries:** in place of 0.1.0's `files`, each skill has a `type` (`"skill-md"` or `"archive"`), a `url` and a `digest` (`sha256:<hex>`).

`WellKnownSkillSource` reads 0.1.0 only. Here's what `main` at c1e19ca2 does with [taskaid.ai's 0.2.0 index](https://taskaid.ai/.well-known/agent-skills/index.json):

- **A bare domain finds nothing.** `hermes skills search https://taskaid.ai` looks for `/.well-known/skills/index.json` and finds no skills. It only works with the full index URL.
- **`url` is ignored.** Fetch builds `<index dir>/<name>/SKILL.md`, which only works when the publisher uses that layout. A skill served from a CDN or a versioned path can't be fetched, and a `type: "archive"` entry can't be installed.
- **`digest` is ignored.** Downloads aren't verified, though the RFC says clients MUST verify and MUST NOT use unverified content. `current_revision` also returns `""`, so `hermes skills check` downloads every skill to compare it.

### Proposed Solution

In `WellKnownSkillSource`:

1. **Discovery:** for a bare domain, try `/.well-known/agent-skills/index.json` first, then fall back to `/.well-known/skills/index.json`.
2. **Version:** branch on `$schema`.
   - The 0.2.0 URI: read each entry's `type`, `url` and `digest`.
   - No `$schema`: keep today's 0.1.0 handling (`files`).
   - An unknown URI: warn and skip the index, as the RFC asks.
3. **`skill-md`:** resolve `url` against the index URL (RFC 3986) and fetch it. Reject the bundle if its SHA-256 doesn't match `digest`.
4. **Updates:** record the entry's `digest` as `source_revision`, and return it from `current_revision`. `skills check` can then skip unchanged skills without downloading them, through the same hook the GitHub source uses.
5. **`archive`:** this could be a follow-up. It might reuse the zip handling in `skills_hub_clawhub.py`, plus the RFC's archive safety rules: no `..` or absolute paths, no links that resolve outside the skill, and a limit on unpacked size.

### Alternatives Considered

Staying on 0.1.0 only. A 0.2.0 publisher then works only when its `url` happens to match the old layout, and nothing gets verified.

### Feature Type

Other

### Scope

Medium (few files, < 300 lines). Archive support would add to that.

issues.title: [Feature]: Live token generation speed (tok/s) in the status bar — attribute slow turns to Hermes vs the LLM
issues.body:
## Problem

**I can't tell whether Hermes or the LLM backend is the performance bottleneck.**

When a response streams in slowly, I have no way to attribute the slowdown. The Hermes TUI currently only shows token *counts* (e.g. `12k tok` context usage in the status bar, or the `finalDetails` token tally at the end of a turn) — there is **no live token-rate readout**. So when a turn crawls, the finger naturally lands on Hermes ("Hermes is slow, it's the agent"), when in fact the slowness may be entirely the **upstream model serving tokens slowly** (or vice versa).

Being able to see the *actual* generation throughput would make this **一目了然** (obvious at a glance):
- **High tok/s but slow wall-clock turn** → the slowness is Hermes-side (tool calls, context processing, post-processing).
- **Low tok/s** → the LLM backend / network is the bottleneck.

This matters most for **self-hosted / vLLM-backed / OpenAI-compatible endpoints** (which I use), where inference speed varies a lot with load and hardware, and where you really want to sanity-check that your serving config is actually fast.

## Proposed Solution

Add an optional **live token-rate readout** in the TUI status bar (`StatusRule` in `ui-tui/src/components/appChrome.tsx`), shown *while streaming is active*.

- Compute and display `X.X tok/s` from the streamed output delta divided by wall-clock time.
- Suggested config key: `display.show_token_speed` (default `off`), mirroring the existing `display.*` booleans so it's opt-in and zero-cost when disabled.
- When enabled, render a segment in the status-bar tail, e.g. `▪ 45.2 tok/s`.
- The server-side `Usage` struct (`input`/`output`/`total`) could optionally carry a timing field (e.g. `elapsed_ms`) so the client can compute an accurate rate; alternatively the client can timestamps the arrival of stream chunks and compute the rate locally (no backend change needed, but only reflects what has been received so far).

## Alternatives Considered

- **vLLM's server-side `/metrics` throughput** — useful, but provider-specific and not visible anywhere in the Hermes UI flow. Doesn't help answer "was it Hermes or the model?" from the terminal you're already looking at.
- **A `/speed` slash command** — only gives a post-hoc snapshot, not live attribution during a slow stream.
- **Client-side timer computing tok/s from streamed chunks** — simplest, no backend change; only reflects received tokens (fine for a "how fast is this generation going" gauge).

## Feature Type

Configuration option

## Scope

Small (single file, < 50 lines)

issues.title: [Bug]: ComfyUI HTTP helper retries unknown-outcome workflow submissions

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: P2
labels.description: Medium — degraded but workaround exists

issues.body:
## Component and scope

`optional-skills/creative/comfyui/scripts/_common.py:http_request` in NousResearch/hermes-agent retries a workflow submission even when the server may already have received it. This is a client correctness issue; no real duplicate charge or production incident is claimed.

Source inspected: main commit `0431192d69d4afd2443a7da15bb9e129a424414c`. The complete `_common.py` and `run_workflow.py` bytes match the earlier tested source at `bf0203a794a07aac3ff764972ab9087baa4e4f4e`:

- `_common.py` SHA256 `9cc7cb65f7b0dd313d5271bc8b7d8eeff8a91d46dde0ffaca25fd82f2e0a78cf`.
- `run_workflow.py` SHA256 `e6a80c11a596123681645d49d951a75afc8fc561bc6b1e890cc67da1a66ff5d1`.

The current source was inspected, not executed as a new whole-branch test run.

## Failure and expected behavior

`ComfyRunner.submit()` builds a payload containing `prompt` and `client_id`, then calls `http_post()` without a special retry budget. `http_request()` defaults to three attempts and retries its listed HTTP statuses and connection/timeout errors without checking the method or body. A server can receive the first POST, lose its response, and then receive the same submission again. `client_id` routes events; it is not a verified submission-deduplication contract.

The recorded isolated reproduction used the real caller and complete transport module with synthetic workflow data and a loopback server that read the POST body and closed the connection before replying. Each transport branch received three POSTs on the original source and one with the candidate, while the failure still reached the caller. Separate recorded cases exercised retryable statuses and ordinary bodyless GET recovery. This evidence used CPython 3.14.7 and requests 2.33.0; it did not call Comfy Cloud, run a model, read real credentials or measure charges.

A response failure must remain an unknown submission outcome, not be reclassified as proof of rejection. Preserve bounded retries for bodyless GET/HEAD/OPTIONS. Do not automatically replay an upload stream or any other body-bearing request without a specific safe-replay contract.

## Relationship to existing work

#145545 owns the operator-facing wait-timeout hint **after** submission. This report concerns the transport loop **inside** a submission attempt, not a second call from the wait loop. Its scope does not replace or expand that hint-only patch. In particular, “the wait loop does not resubmit” must not be read as “the transport never retries a POST.” #143365 changes a different workflow-repair helper and two guidance files; it does not change this transport loop. Bounded open/closed indexed searches found no exact repair owner for this delta; that is not an exhaustive claim about unindexed work.

## Proposed narrow change

The patch below extracts only the retry change and its documentation from an existing reviewed candidate. The executable `http_request` body matches that candidate; no other function is changed. The extraction was applied and reversed against the byte-identical source and checked structurally. It has **not** been rerun as a separate behavior suite, and no full-suite or current-environment certification is claimed.

This conservative policy also stops retrying POST after a refused connection or HTTP 429/503. Those cases can sometimes be recoverable, but the generic transport does not have a verified distinction or idempotency contract. Normal readiness GETs continue to retry. An explicit caller-owned safe-replay contract, if wanted later, is a separate change rather than a reason to repeat an unknown submission now.

## Patch

```diff
--- a/optional-skills/creative/comfyui/scripts/_common.py
+++ b/optional-skills/creative/comfyui/scripts/_common.py
@@ -440,8 +440,10 @@
     """Single entry point for all HTTP traffic.
 
     Behavior:
-      - Retries on connection errors and on HTTP statuses in RETRY_STATUS_CODES,
-        with exponential backoff + jitter.
+      - Retries bodyless GET/HEAD/OPTIONS on connection errors and HTTP statuses
+        in RETRY_STATUS_CODES, with exponential backoff + jitter. Other requests
+        get one attempt: a lost POST response does not prove it was rejected,
+        and consumed upload streams cannot be replayed safely.
       - For cross-host redirects, drops Authorization-style headers (so signed
         URLs don't leak the API key to S3/CloudFront).
       - When `stream=True` and `sink` is a Path, streams the response body to
@@ -462,6 +464,13 @@
                 "Multipart upload requires the `requests` package. "
                 "Install with: pip install requests"
             )
+
+    # No caller supplies an idempotency guarantee for workflow submission.
+    # client_id routes events; it is not a submission deduplication key.
+    if method.upper() not in {"GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"} or any(
+        body is not None for body in (json_body, data, files, form)
+    ):
+        retries = min(retries, 1)
 
     last_exc: Exception | None = None
     for attempt in range(retries):
```
