prs.title: feat(plugins): expose the semantic colour roles to plugin themes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

#8071 asks for a plugin theme extension point. #8422 landed the first slice:
six roles (`bg`, `surface`, `surface-raised`, `border`, `text`,
`text-secondary`). Those cover the page frame, but not the semantic colour
surface a theme actually has to touch — a plugin that wants its own accent,
status colours, or the lower-contrast text and border tiers still has to reach
into raw `--app-*` names, which this closed API deliberately rejects.

This PR widens the closed set to the 31 semantic colour roles that
`console/src/styles/tokens.css` already defines and the console already
consumes, and keeps the compatibility story honest:

- the original six roles keep their current minimum SDK version, so plugins
  that already call `overrideTokens` are unaffected;
- the new roles sit behind `sdk.version >= 1.2.0` plus a `themeTokens`
  capability, so a plugin cannot silently depend on a role that an older host
  does not know.

Group 2 from #8071 (fifteen shape and layer roles: radius, shadow,
focus-ring, scrollbar, fill) stays out of this PR and is left for a separate
discussion, as requested.

## Evidence

Every role below is already read by the console. No component was changed and
no new colour was invented — this only opens roles that exist.

| family | role | representative consumer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| surface | `surface-subtle` | `layouts/index.module.less:324` |
| surface | `surface-sunken` | `components/RenderableCodeBlock/index.module.less:122` |
| surface | `shell-bg` | `layouts/dockableSidebar.module.less:13` |
| text | `text-tertiary` | `layouts/dockableSidebar.module.less:36` |
| text | `text-quaternary` | `layouts/index.module.less:254` |
| border | `border-subtle` | `layouts/index.module.less:53` |
| border | `border-strong` | `layouts/sidebarA.module.less:99` |
| accent | `accent` | `App.tsx:421` |
| accent | `accent-hover` | `App.tsx:422` |
| accent | `accent-soft` | `App.tsx:423` |
| status | `success-bg` | `components/LoopInput/index.module.less:57` |
| status | `warning-border` | `components/Chat/ToolCards/shared/offloadBanner.module.less:11` |
| status | `error-text` | `tauri/BackendLoadingPage.module.less:52` |

Both schemes are exercised rather than assumed: `themeTokens.test.ts` asserts
each role lands in the `:root` block with its light value and in the
`html.dark-mode` block with its dark value.

## Self-review

1. Overlapping registrations — `install.test.ts` keeps the existing
   "stacks per token and falls back on dispose" case, and the new semantic
   roles go through the same stacking path.
2. Switching scheme or preset while an override is active —
   `themeTokens.integration.test.ts` keeps "wins over the preset's inline
   `--app-surface` in both schemes" and "restores the preset when the plugin is
   unloaded".
3. Cleanup — "removes the element once every override is gone" and
   `disposeAll(pluginId)` both still clear the new roles.
4. Invalid input — a role missing one scheme and a genuinely unknown name both
   still throw; the unknown-name case now uses `not-a-role` so it does not
   accidentally test a role that became valid in this PR.
5. Backward compatibility — `sdk.version: 1.0.0` stays valid for the original
   six roles; `1.1.0` with `themeTokens` is rejected with a clear message;
   `1.2.0` with `themeTokens` is accepted.

## Test scope

- Console: `src/plugins` — 34 files, 459 passed, including the
  capability-gate cases, the out-of-order catalog regression and the PEP 440
  epoch case.
- Python: `tests/unit/app/routers` 1114 passed, 17 skipped, 2 failed and
  `tests/unit/plugins/test_sdk_entry_contract.py` passed. Both failures are
  `test_config_router.py` cases that need `src/qwenpaw/official_channels/`
  `index.json`; that path is generated, is not tracked in the checkout, and
  the two cases raise `FileNotFoundError` before reaching anything this PR
  touches.
- `tsc -b --noEmit`, eslint, prettier and pre-commit on the touched files.
- Browser: `python scripts/verify_theme_tokens.py` from `console/` (values in
  the follow-up section below).

## Coordination with #8764

#8764 also moves `SDK_VERSION` to `1.2.0` and touches
`src/qwenpaw/plugins/frontend/index.d.ts`. This PR needs the same version slot.
Whichever lands first, the other rebases onto it — the two changes are additive
and share only that version line, so the rebase is mechanical. If #8764 lands
first, this PR moves to 1.2.1; the gate reads `>= 1.2.0`, so the bump changes
no behaviour.


## Review follow-up

Five rounds are folded into `48fb8f1b`.

**One compatibility decision on both list paths.** The loader rejects an
incompatible SDK declaration before a plugin loads, but `/frontend_plugin`'s
disk fallback forwarded the manifest verbatim, so the console became the only
judge. `1.2.0rc1` and `1.2.0.dev1` are below 1.2.0 under PEP 440 and may not
carry `themeTokens`, yet the console's numeric comparison read them as 1.2.0
and accepted the extended roles. Both paths now call `_sdk_declaration()`,
which runs `validate_sdk()` and reports "not declared" when the declaration is
invalid. A pre-release without `themeTokens` is still forwarded unchanged, and
the six original roles need no declaration at all. Covered by
`test_frontend_list_rejects_incompatible_prerelease_on_disk[1.2.0rc1|1.2.0.dev1]`,
`test_frontend_list_keeps_a_prerelease_without_extended_capabilities` and
`test_frontend_list_applies_the_same_check_when_loaded`.

**The gate covers undeclared usage.** `validate_sdk` used to run only when a
plugin declared `themeTokens`, so a plugin could use a new role while declaring
nothing at all. `/frontend_plugin` now carries `sdk_version` and
`sdk_capabilities`, and `chat.theme.overrideTokens` consults that declaration
for every extended role: no declaration, an older version, or a missing
capability each throw with the role, the plugin, what is required and what was
declared. A manifest that cannot be read is treated as undeclared, so the check
fails closed. The original six roles keep their 1.0.0 minimum and need no
declaration.

**Components demonstrate it through the public API.** `themeVerify/main.tsx`
registers through `chat.theme.overrideTokens()` and disposes the handle it
returns; the internal store is not touched on the success path. Playwright
reads `getComputedStyle` for nine roles in both schemes — `bg`, `surface`,
`border`, `text`, `accent`, `error-text`, `success-bg`, `warning-border`,
`info-text` — plus the card, button and text probes: 23 expectations, no
failures. The harness also writes the user preset inline on `<html>` the way
`App.tsx` does, applies an override, changes the preset while it is active and
then disposes: the override keeps winning during the change, and after dispose
the page shows the *new* preset (`rgb(42, 42, 42)`), not the earlier one.
Stacked registrations still walk back across two disposes, and the same public
call with an undeclared plugin throws in the browser too.

Third-party scope is documented in `plugins/frontend/README.md`: this is a
colour surface, not a full UI theme. Only the listed roles participate, and
layout, spacing, typography, iconography, chart palettes and markup that
hardcodes `rgb()`/`rgba()` do not follow the override.

**A stale plugin list no longer clears a fresh declaration.** `fetchFrontendPlugins()`
stamps each list request with a monotonic id and only lets the newest request
rewrite the shared registry; an older response that resolves late is still
returned to its own caller but no longer overwrites newer declarations.
`executePluginScript()` additionally writes the `sdk_version` /
`sdk_capabilities` of the record it is about to evaluate back into the
registry before the entry script runs, so a load is bound to the record it came
from even if the shared map changed while the script was in flight. Covered by
`keeps the newest SDK declaration when an older list arrives late`, which
drives a deferred stale response and asserts the fresh plugin keeps
`themeTokens`; removing the request-id guard turns it red.

**The frontend no longer re-decides the SDK version.** `meetsMinVersion()` is
gone: `chat.theme.overrideTokens` now asks only whether the declaration carries
the `themeTokens` capability, which is the decision the backend already made
under PEP 440. `accepts a PEP 440 epoch version the backend already validated`
pins `0!1.2.0` as accepted, and the backend side of that premise is asserted in
`test_theme_tokens_capability_gates_on_sdk_version`. Re-introducing a raw-string
version comparison turns the epoch case red.

prs.title: fix(console): restore native scrolling in the chat transcript
prs.body:
## Description

The chat transcript used to intercept every wheel event and scroll by hand, so
mouse-wheel scrolling lost its native momentum and felt choppy.

- `console/src/pages/Chat/index.tsx`: remove the capture-phase, `passive: false`
  wheel listener that called `preventDefault()` and wrote `scrollTop` from the
  main thread (#6904). The vendor bubble list already scrolls natively —
  keyboard scrolling still moves the same `[-max, 0]` range of the
  `column-reverse` list — so wheel input goes through compositor scrolling
  again and keeps its inertia.
- `console/src/pages/Chat/HostBubbles.module.less`: clamp the bubble content
  wrapper so a wide Markdown table resolves its own `max-width` against the
  bubble instead of an oversized shrink-to-fit parent, whose overflow
  `overflow-x: hidden` then clipped. Wide tables now get a horizontal scrollbar
  inside the bubble.
- `console/src/pages/Chat/index.module.less`: drop the floating header
  `backdrop-filter: blur(10px)`. The header is absolutely positioned over the
  scroller (54px tall, 1151px wide), so the blur re-rasterized ~62k px of
  scrolling content on every frame; it now uses the opaque surface color.

**Related Issue:** Relates to #6904.

**Security Considerations:** none. Frontend-only change; no new input parsing,
no data flow, no config or credential handling.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix

## Component(s) Affected

- [x] Console (frontend web UI)

## Testing

Open a long chat session in the console and scroll with the mouse wheel (or
trackpad): the transcript should scroll with native momentum and no stepping.
Then narrow the window and open a chat containing a wide Markdown table: the
table scrolls horizontally inside the bubble instead of being clipped on the
right.

`npx vitest run src/pages/Chat/messageScroll.test.ts` covers the scroll-range
helper and passes.

## Evidence

Wheel events are no longer consumed by JS — same synthetic event, before and
after the change, on a live console session:

```
# injected probe: dispatch a wheel event inside the transcript
el.dispatchEvent(new WheelEvent('wheel', { deltaY: -120, cancelable: true, bubbles: true }))
# before this PR: event.defaultPrevented === true, scroller.scrollTop === -120 (written by the handler)
# after this PR:  event.defaultPrevented === false
```

Unit tests:

```
$ npx vitest run src/pages/Chat/messageScroll.test.ts
 ✓ src/pages/Chat/messageScroll.test.ts (9 tests) 91ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  9 passed (9)
   Duration  1.08s (transform 44ms, setup 105ms, import 61ms, tests 91ms, environment 672ms)
```

Build, bundle budget unchanged:

```
Initial Brotli         0.823 MiB / 1.200 MiB
Each initial JS raw    2.196 MiB / 2.500 MiB
verify:monaco-css      OK (135 CSS files)
```

Screenshot of the wide-table fix on the same console build: pasted below.

`console/src/pages/Chat/messageScroll.ts` and its test are left untouched; the
app no longer references them. Happy to delete both in this PR if you prefer.

prs.title: fix(console): repair CJK emphasis boundaries in chat Markdown
prs.body:
## What problem this solves `**中文。**后面` and `__中文！__后面` never parse: CommonMark only accepts a closing delimiter run that is right-flanking, and a run preceded by CJK punctuation and followed by a CJK letter is neither right- nor left-flanking. The renderer therefore shows the raw markers instead of bold text. The Markdown source is never rewritten. The fix is one instance-level marked tokenizer extension. ## Scope Type: C (new renderer behaviour, no data or protocol change) | Input | Stock | This PR | |---|---|---| | `**甲。**乙` | literal markers | `甲。乙` | | `__甲。__乙` | literal markers | `甲。乙` | | `**甲，**乙` … `**甲？**乙` | literal markers | `甲，乙` | | single `*甲。*乙` / `_甲。_乙` | literal | unchanged | | ASCII punctuation before the closer (`**甲.**乙`) | literal | unchanged | | ASCII follower (`**甲。**b`, `**甲。**1`) | literal | unchanged | | nested or unbalanced runs (`***甲。***乙`) | stock result | unchanged | | CJK punctuation after the closer (`**甲。**，`) | stock result | unchanged | | already-valid emphasis before a CJK span (`**标准** **甲。**乙`) | two spans | two spans | | fenced code, inline code, HTML | verbatim | verbatim | | link label and image alt | verbatim | verbatim | | link `href` / `title`, image `src` / `alt` / `title` | unchanged | unchanged | | tables | literal in cells | emphasis in cells | Where the extension does not take over, the stock tokenizer result is used unchanged. ## How it works `console/src/utils/markdownCjkStrong.ts` registers one `tokenizer.emStrong` override: - it runs only when the source starts with `**` or `__`; - `findCandidate` accepts only the agreed shape — CJK punctuation before the closer, CJK letter after it — and takes exactly one candidate. If the span contains an inline character that may belong to another construct (`` ` ``, `$`, `<`, `~`, `[`, `\(`, a bare URL), it returns `false` at once and the stock tokenizer owns the span. That single guard covers code spans, formulas, HTML, strikethrough, links and images without tracking any of them separately; - when the candidate survives that guard, `findCloserAroundInlineNodes` looks for the closer outside any *complete* inline node, using marked's own `codespan` and `link` tokenizers so a closer inside a code span or a link is not taken; - `indexSuffixBalance` scans the same masked source once, from the end, with marked's own closer rules per delimiter, and records for every offset how many markers the stock parser could still match after it. The extension only takes over when that index proves the native parser cannot close the run; otherwise it returns `false`; - the body is limited to 4096 characters. `console/src/components/ChatMarkdown/ChatMarkdown.tsx` is a local counterpart of the SDK's Markdown component. The SDK builds its `config` internally and never forwards one, so the only way to register an instance-level extension without touching global tokenizer prototypes is to compose the same pieces ourselves: math, footnotes, citations, streaming cursor, media, link handling, HTML sanitisation and the code-block slot are all preserved, and the only difference from the SDK is the extra extension. `AssistantMarkdown` renders through it; `vite.config.ts` inlines the SDK subpaths the wrapper imports so the unit tests resolve them the same way the app does. ## Known limitation The extension does not only recover delimiters the native parser left unconsumed. When it takes over a span that contains a run the native parser *did* consume, it re-pairs: `**甲。**乙**丙，**丁` - stock: `**甲。乙丙，**丁` - this PR: `甲。乙丙，丁` The stock result already bolds `乙`; this PR splits that pairing and bolds `甲。` and `丙，` instead. Recovering more CJK text is not worth changing input the parser renders correctly today, so this revision is held rather than merged. ## Evidence - `console/src/utils/markdownCjkStrong.test.tsx`: 90 tests through the real renderer — `XMarkdown` for the emphasis cases (agreed punctuation family, follower family, protected regions, repeat-render stability, streamed-versus-complete equality, two-span preservation) and `ChatMarkdown` for the formula cases (one KaTeX node with its payload, and a closer inside a formula producing no emphasis), plus cost guards on the scan and on native fallback. - `console/src/pages/Chat/AssistantMarkdown.test.tsx` and `HostBubbles.render.test.tsx`: 22 tests pass, covering the streamed code-block pipeline that this component reuses. - Headless Chrome, 1,000 repetitions of `**状态。**正常
` (measured by the reviewer): | version | time | |---|---| | this PR | ~38 ms | | recovery after native parsing, fast rejection index | 455 ms | | token-only | 874 ms | - `tsc -b --noEmit`, eslint and prettier pass on the changed files. ## Test scope - Target: `console/src/utils/markdownCjkStrong.test.tsx` (90 passed) - Neighbour: `console/src/pages/Chat/AssistantMarkdown.test.tsx`, `HostBubbles.render.test.tsx` (22 passed) - `tsc -b --noEmit`, eslint and prettier pass on the changed files. ## Status Held per review. The focused rendering tests and the three benchmarks (space-, `
`- and colon-separated inputs, including streaming updates) stay in the branch as the record of the problem. Two directions were named in review and neither is in this PR: reducing the repeated scans at the parser layer, and letting the Chat SDK accept Markdown extensions so a local renderer copy is not needed. The first is outside this repository; the second is a separate improvement.

prs.body:
<!-- rw-base-touch2 -->

## What Problem This Solves

`check_local_whisper_available()` imported whisper merely to decide whether the optional dependency is installed. Importing whisper pulls in torch and the CUDA runtime, ~690 MB RSS in our measurements (163 MB → 853 MB), never released because Python imports are permanent.

The probe backs `GET /api/workspace/local-whisper-status`, which the Console calls when the Voice Transcription settings page mounts, even for a remote Whisper API or when transcription is disabled. One visit inflated an otherwise idle qwenpaw process to ~1.9 GB PSS.

## Evidence

Switched the probe to `importlib.util.find_spec()` (filesystem lookup, ~0 MB). Real import errors still surface when local transcription runs, because the model loader imports whisper for real.

Unit tests in `tests/unit/agents/utils/test_audio_transcription.py` assert the probe never imports whisper and that a missing spec is reported as not installed.

prs.title: fix(plugins): log unhandled errors in RPC request handlers
prs.body:
## Description

`RpcPeer._dispatch_request` (`src/qwenpaw/plugins/execution/rpc.py`) catches any unexpected handler exception, replies with `-32603 internal error` / `INTERNAL_ERROR`, and then discards the exception (`_ = exc`). Nothing is logged, so a worker-side failure such as the `RESPONSE_SCOPE_LIMIT` error in the linked issue shows up only as a generic "internal error" with no traceback (the reporter had to patch `rpc.py` locally to see it).

This PR adds a module logger and calls `logger.exception(...)` (method name + traceback) in that `except Exception` branch before replying. The reply sent to the caller is unchanged.

**Related Issue:** Relates to #8814. This covers only suggested fix 3 (do not discard exceptions in `rpc.py`); the route-eviction problem (fixes 1 and 2) is a design decision left to the maintainers, so the issue should stay open.

prs.title: fix(channels): keep Discord code fences balanced at chunk boundaries
prs.body:
## Description

Discord `chunk_text` toggled the code-fence state before deciding whether to flush. When the opening fence of a code block was the line that overflowed the chunk, `_flush()` treated the previous chunk as inside a fence and appended a stray closing fence. The next chunk then started with a reopener plus the original opener, so the opener appeared twice. Both messages rendered wrong.

The fix keeps the fence state from before the current line and uses it for the flush and the reopen. It then applies the toggle. Lines that don't trigger a flush behave as before.

**Related Issue:** Fixes #8870

prs.title: fix(media): enforce the inline budget, rescale after a refusal, and report omissions
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The downscale pass added in #8632 judged an image by its longest side alone. Three gaps followed from that, and they are fixed together because they meet on the same path.

**1. The byte budget and the side limit are two independent limits.**
A 2000x2000 PNG is well inside the 8192 px side limit and can still weigh 11.46 MiB, so the pass returned it untouched and the formatter rejected the request on bytes right afterwards. Both limits are now checked, and a formatter that provisions its own limits passes them down, so this pass and the cap cannot disagree about what fits.

**2. PNG has no quality knob.**
Every quality step emitted the same bytes and paid for another full deflate. The quality loop is skipped for PNG; only reducing the side makes it smaller.

**3. A rejection could not name the image it rejected.**
The retry log said "some media" while every image in the request was dropped, which left no way to tell which one the provider objected to. Each wire media block now gets a label (position, media type, decoded size) across the Anthropic `source`, OpenAI `image_url` and Gemini `inline_data`/`file_data` spellings, and the log names them.

**4. A rejection that named the media was replayed forever.**
Non-streaming recovery recognised only `413` / body-size wording. A `400 image dimensions exceed the maximum allowed size` fell through to `raise`, and because the offending block stayed in `state.context`, every later turn sent it again and collected the same rejection. The streaming path did strip media, but only for that one request — the identical loop, one turn later.

Both paths now classify a payload refusal, mark the historical copies as omitted once (`mark_media_omitted_after_overflow`) and retry. The stored message keeps its bytes, so the full-resolution file stays retrievable; only request copies are stripped.

**5. When the refusal is about the active turn, shrinking beats deleting.**
If nothing historical can be omitted, the refusal is about the image the user is asking about. Deleting it would be wrong. The request-scoped limits (`max_image_side`, `max_bytes`) are halved once for a single retry and restored afterwards, so the retry sends a smaller rendition while the stored message is untouched.

**6. Dropped media was invisible to the user.**
When media is replaced by a text placeholder the model answers as if the file had never been attached — indistinguishable from "the model ignored my image". The reply now carries `qwenpaw_media_omitted` (`{count, reason}`), which the Console renders as one system line and non-Console channels send as one extra text line.

## Scope

Type: B (state machine / retry), with a D-shaped surface because the notice crosses agents → channels → console.

- `src/qwenpaw/providers/capping_formatter.py` — `MAX_IMAGE_SIDE` moves here, beside the byte cap, so both media limits have one home; new `max_image_side` field (`ge=0`, default 8192).
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/utils/image_resize.py` — two limits decided independently, `max_side` threaded through, quality loop skipped for PNG.
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/model_factory.py` — reads the formatter's limits and passes them down; new `_describe_wire_media_blocks` / `_wire_media_label`.
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/utils/message_request_normalizer.py` — threads `max_bytes` / `max_side` to the resize pass.
- `src/qwenpaw/agents/react_agent.py` — payload-refusal classification on the non-streaming path, one-shot limit tightening with restore, per-response omission notice.
- `src/qwenpaw/app/channels/base.py` — `_media_omitted_notice`, sent with the existing fallback notice so channels without Console rendering see it too.
- `console/src/pages/Chat/fallbackNotice.ts`, `console/src/pages/Chat/index.tsx`, `console/src/locales/{en,zh}.json` — parse and render the notice.

## Self-review

1. **Callers of `downscale_image_bytes`** — `_rescale_source` is the only intermediate, `normalize_messages_for_model_request_async` the only entry point; both are updated, and both keep the old behaviour when the new keyword arguments are omitted (`max_side=MAX_IMAGE_SIDE`, `max_bytes=MAX_INLINE_MEDIA_BYTES`).
2. **`MAX_IMAGE_SIDE` relocation** — `grep -rn MAX_IMAGE_SIDE src/` returns only `capping_formatter.py` (definition) and the modules that import it; no stale constant remains in `image_resize`.
3. **`max_image_side` as a new field** — declared with `ge=0` and the same default as before (8192), so every existing formatter subclass inherits it; `_normalize_messages_for_formatter` reads it with `getattr(..., MAX_IMAGE_SIDE)` so a custom formatter without the field still works.
4. **`_describe_wire_media_blocks`** — used only by `QwenPawAgent._last_wire_media_summary`, which returns `[]` when no formatter is active.
5. **Reversal** — `max_bytes <= 0` keeps its old meaning of "no byte limit" rather than shrinking forever.
6. **Both limits agree** — the resize pass receives `formatter.max_bytes` / `formatter.max_image_side` instead of the module constants, so a provider override cannot make the pass shrink to a different budget than the one enforced a moment later.
7. **Bounded retries** — both refusals share one budget (`max_recoveries`): a retry that is refused again recovers once more from the same budget instead of ending the turn, and a recovery that re-raises its own exception stops immediately. Limit tightening is one-shot per user turn: `_qwenpaw_media_limits_tightened_this_turn` blocks a second shrink after the borrowed pair is restored, so the same request shape is not sent twice, and `_reply()` resets it for the next turn.
8. **Stored history is not rewritten** — the omission pass only writes `qwenpaw_omitted_media_ids` metadata. `test_omissions_survive_resume_and_allow_new_images` verifies the state round-trips and a newly attached image is still sent.
9. **The notice is additive** — with no omission the channel output is byte-identical to the previous string (a single fallback line). An unparsable notice renders nothing rather than an empty system message.
10. **Non-streaming classifier stays narrow** — `is_request_body_too_large` is untouched (still `413` / body-size only); the media branch is a separate condition that additionally requires media on the wire and the existing payload-rejection classifier.

## Test scope

- Targeted: `test_context_overflow_recovery.py` + `test_react_agent_media_strip.py` + `test_media_omitted_notice.py` + `test_message_request_normalizer.py` + `test_image_resize.py` + `tests/unit/app/channels` — **383 passed, 7 failed**. The seven are the pre-existing video cases (`test_video_rejection_recovers_and_next_turn_skips_video`, `test_mixed_media_rejection_uses_media_free_retry`, `test_positive_video_limit_does_not_disable_next_valid_input`, `test_failed_video_retry_does_not_learn_or_mutate_history`, `test_video_cache_expires_and_is_scoped_to_model`); they fail the same way on the base revision, which I re-ran to confirm.
- Adjacent: `tests/unit/agents -k 'media or overflow or omitt'` — **466 passed, 3 skipped, 15 failed**. Seven are the video cases above; the other eight are `test_view_media` audio/video conversions, which fail identically when the suite runs against the PR base source (`8c7c3127`) — local ffmpeg behaviour, not this PR.
- Console: `fallbackNotice.test.ts` — **6 passed**; `sdkHostIntegration.test.tsx` + `ChatPage.coverage.test.tsx` — **196 passed**; `tsc -b --noEmit` clean; `prettier --check` clean
- `pre-commit run --files <changed files>` — all hooks passed (black reformatted two test files on the first pass, clean on the re-run)

## Evidence

A 2000x2000 high-entropy PNG, well inside the side limit and far over the byte cap:

```
INPUT   side=2000x2000  bytes=12,015,257  (11.46 MiB)
        longest side 2000 <= 8192 -> the old side-only check returned this unchanged
OUTPUT  bytes=596,065  (0.57 MiB)  media_type=image/png  changed=True
        under 2 MiB cap: True

max_bytes=0 -> unchanged=True  (11.46 MiB)
```

The media labels, one per wire spelling:

```
#1 image/png 1.0 MiB      (Anthropic source)
#1 image/jpeg 1.0 MiB     (OpenAI image_url data URL)
#1 image/webp 1.0 MiB     (Gemini inline_data)
```

The refusal path, measured before and after the change:

```
before  marked=0  max_image_side=8192  qwenpaw_media_omitted=ABSENT
after   marked=8  max_image_side=8192 (history had blocks to omit)

active-turn only:
before  marked=0  side=8192 bytes=2097152
retry   side=4096 bytes=1048576
after   side=8192 bytes=2097152 (restored)
```

Removing the new classifier turns two tests red; removing the streaming omission call turns one red — both restored afterwards.

Every fix in this revision was falsified on its own: reverting the recovery loop, the resize-ineffective gate, the audio-count branch, the omit-keeps-active-image condition, the per-turn notice dedupe, or the tool-parameters short circuit each turns exactly its own test red, and the code is restored afterwards.

Refs #8632, #8629

issues.body:
### Tracker kind roadmap / epic tracker ### Purpose This tracker coordinates splitting `crates/zeroclaw-runtime` into smaller crates, and the decision about which modules are meant to stay in it. It holds the open decisions, the order of the pull requests, and who has taken each one. An analysis, a plan and a working proof are in one folder: https://github.com/JordanTheJet/zeroclaw/tree/docs/runtime-detangle-plan/docs/maintainers/runtime-crate-split. Start with `REPORT.md`, which is one screen. Everything was measured at `master` commit `e02b7fb6f6` on 2026-11-22. It is a proposal, and nothing in it is decided. **The crate today.** Numbers in boxes are thousands of production lines. Solid arrows are the intended direction of calls. Dotted arrows are the 42 references that point the wrong way, each with its count. `agent` and `tools` refer to each other 26 and 64 times, which is why they stay together. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph hosts["Hosts: call the core, are not called by it"] rpc["rpc 24.6K"] daemon["daemon 3.4K"] doctor["doctor 2.1K"] hostmisc["service, tunnel, relay, enroll, heartbeat,
restart, integrations, migration"] end subgraph core["Core: one unit"] agent["agent 29.9K"] tools["tools 21.5K"] skills["skills 7.2K"] comp["composition 0.7K"] approval["approval 0.5K"] end subgraph subs["Subsystems the core calls"] sop["sop 24.1K"] security["security 11.2K"] cron["cron 6.3K"] obs["observability 3.3K"] quick["quickstart 2.4K"] plugin["plugin_runtime 1.2K"] hooks["hooks 1.0K"] end subgraph leaves["Leaves: depend on nothing in the crate, or only on each other"] leafset["i18n, util, health, live_config_authority,
control_plane, verifiable_intent, identity, and others"] end hosts --> core core --> subs subs --> leaves agent <-->|"26 / 64"| tools sop -.->|"12"| agent sop -.->|"1"| tools sop -.->|"1"| cron cron -.->|"6"| agent cron -.->|"8"| comp cron -.->|"2"| tools obs -.->|"1"| agent hooks -.->|"2"| agent quick -.->|"4"| agent plugin -.->|"3"| tools security -.->|"2"| sop ``` **The proposed split.** Arrows read "depends on". A thick border means built and compile-checked. A dashed border means proposed and not decided. A dotted border means not designed yet. About 4K lines (`quickstart`, `hooks`, `browse`, `routines`, `trust`) are left for later and not drawn. ```mermaid %%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 420}}}%% flowchart TB hostcr["Host crates, new
daemon, heartbeat, restart, doctor,
service, tunnel, integrations,
migration, later relay and enroll
about 14.6K
Status: not designed"] rt["zeroclaw-runtime after the split
about 107K
agent, tools, skills, composition,
approval, security, rpc, i18n,
plugin_runtime, plugin_state,
live_config_authority, control_plane,
config_application, small helpers
Status: proposed, the RFC decides"] obsc["zeroclaw-observability, new
observability, 3.3K
Status: built"] cronc["zeroclaw-cron, new
cron, 6.3K
Status: not designed,
design note first"] sopc["zeroclaw-sop, new
sop and calendar, 24.3K
Status: not designed"] infra["zeroclaw-infra, exists
gains util, health, shell_output
about 0.4K
Status: util built, the rest proposed"] prov["zeroclaw-providers, exists
gains the redaction helpers
about 0.3K
Status: built, home not decided"] hostcr --> rt rt --> obsc rt --> cronc rt --> sopc rt --> infra rt --> prov obsc --> infra obsc --> prov classDef built stroke-width:3px; classDef proposed stroke-dasharray:6 4; classDef undesigned stroke-dasharray:2 3; class obsc,infra,prov built; class rt proposed; class hostcr,cronc,sopc undesigned; ``` What it found: - **The crate is three layers.** It has 160,631 production lines. 42 references point up from seven subsystems into the core. `agent` and `tools` are one unit and stay together. - **The exceptions come from two documents that disagree.** 55 of the 60 rows in the exception table in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/AGENTS.md` send code to `zeroclaw-kernel`, a crate nothing schedules. FND-001 assigns the agent loop, security policy, plugin host and IPC API to `zeroclaw-runtime`. The holding-crate contract lists the agent loop, security and skills for extraction. - **A module moved without editing its files breaks few open pull requests.** Against all 588 open pull requests, moving `cron` byte-for-byte breaks 0 of the 23 that merge today. The same move with path edits inside the files breaks 9. For `sop` it is 1 against 12. - **The first three moves are built.** They pass `cargo check` on the workspace with default features, with OpenTelemetry added and with no default features, and they pass `cargo fmt --check`. Tests, clippy and rustdoc have not run on them. Together they break 9 of the 112 open pull requests that touch the same files and merge today. What is designed and what is not: - **Designed and built:** the move method and the first three moves. - **Proposed, not decided:** the target layout. About 107K of the 161K production lines would stay as the crate's core, about 49K would leave, and about 4K are undecided. Which modules stay is the RFC question. - **Not designed:** the cron execution seam, and the host and SOP moves. `PLAN.md` marks the last two as not ready to schedule. The conflict counts are textual. A pull request that still merges may fail to compile after a move, and the measurement assumes GitHub merges the way local git 2.43 does. The analysis went through five adversarial review passes. `REVIEW-LOG.md` has each verdict and what it changed, and `README.md` says how the work was produced. ### Scope and non-goals In scope: - [ ] Decide whether to open an RFC on which modules stay in `zeroclaw-runtime` (first decision below) - [ ] Move `util` into `zeroclaw-infra` (5 files, +7/−2) - [ ] Give credential redaction one owner below the agent loop (7 files, +54/−52) - [ ] Extract `observability` into its own crate (19 files, +100/−6; 11 of the 12 moved files are exact renames) - [ ] Bring the move scripts into the repository once they meet the four review conditions in `PLAN.md`, Phase 0 - [ ] List workspace members one per line in the root `Cargo.toml`, which should remove a manifest conflict point (not simulated) - [ ] Cron: a design note on who owns execution admission, then the extraction - [ ] Hosts and SOP: each needs a probe before it can be scheduled - Corrections to the analysis itself Out of scope: - The split of the gateway and the core into separate processes. That is separate work. - The design of the cron execution seam. It needs its own design note, linked from here. - The RFC text. If an RFC is opened, it is filed separately and linked from here. - Behaviour changes. A move changes where code lives, not what it does. ### Linked work - #10546: the cron extraction issue. Its rule that the old path is "deleted, not re-exported or shimmed" is one of the decisions below. - #10557: the cron extraction pull request. The plan recommends keeping it open as the record until a replacement pull request exists, and not rebasing it. - #7432: the tracker that deferred the cron extraction to a later release. - #5574: FND-001. - The folder linked above: `REPORT.md`, `PLAN.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `REVIEW-LOG.md`, the scripts, the measured data and the three patches. ### Routing evidence and next decision Reason to stay open: the work is one governance decision and a sequence of pull requests over several weeks, and each move has to be timed against the open pull requests it touches. Next decisions: 1. **Open the RFC?** It would amend the holding-crate contract so that named resident modules need no exception and only held modules do. This looks like it crosses two RFC triggers: a governance change, and a cross-cutting refactor that changes ownership across established boundaries. Under the proposed list, up to 43 of the 60 exception rows would no longer be needed; 14 of those also cover locale catalogs, whose owner the RFC would have to settle too. It gates none of the moves above. 2. **Open the first three pull requests?** They need no governance decision. Tests, clippy and rustdoc have to run on them first. 3. **Commission the cron design note?** Cron does not start until it settles who owns execution admission. 4. **Relax the rule in #10546** so that a re-export may stay at the old path? That rule forced #10557 to edit about 25 caller files. 5. **Crate names**, which are permanent once published, starting with `zeroclaw-observability`. 6. **Home for the redaction helpers:** `zeroclaw-providers`, which the prototype uses, or `zeroclaw-infra`. Visible owner: the author of this issue, until others take items. ### Close criteria Close when the governance question is decided, each module the plan lists as leaving has either moved or been kept with a recorded reason, and #10546 and #10557 are resolved. Close earlier if a narrower tracker replaces this one. ### Stale-exemption requested? Yes - tracker itself is the active coordination surface

issues.title: [Bug]: `/model <id>` replies "Model switched" but requests keep the profile's configured model

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issues.body: ### Affected component channel ### Severity S2 - degraded behavior ### Current behavior In a chat, `/model ` replies that the model was switched, and `/model` then reports the new id as current. The next request still asks the provider for the model configured on the active provider profile. For a literal ID that matches neither a route hint nor a route model, the next request used the selected ID on the unpinned profile and retained the configured ID on both pinned profiles. I ran this on v0.9.0 (`6c78ba5`) and on master `e02b7fb6f6`, with the same results on both. The config had three provider profiles: `custom.caller` with `model = "caller-model"` (the agent's profile), `custom.other` with `model = "other-model"`, and `custom.nomodel` with no `model`. | Active profile | Message | Reply | `model` in the next request | |---|---|---|---| | `custom.caller`, the agent's own | `/model other-model` | `Model switched to other-model (model_provider: custom.caller). Context preserved.` | `caller-model` | | `custom.other`, after `/models custom.other` | `/model third-model` | `Model switched to third-model (model_provider: custom.other). Context preserved.` | `other-model` | | `custom.nomodel`, after `/models custom.nomodel` | `/model other-model` | `Model switched to other-model (model_provider: custom.nomodel). Context preserved.` | `other-model` | So the profile that sets `model` is the case that breaks, and the profile without one works. After the first row, `/model` replied `Current model: other-model` and listed `session (this chat): custom.caller / other-model`, while requests kept asking for `caller-model`. The `/models` reply has the same mismatch. From a default session, `/models custom.other` replied `Current model is caller-model`, and the next request asked for `other-model`. With `custom.nomodel` as this agent's default, the channel runtime failed to start. On its pinned default, a literal switch to a different, unrouted ID left the request on the configured model. The CLI could start the no-model configuration with an explicit `--model`. ```text Error: agents.main.model_provider Caused by: no model configured: model_provider 'custom.nomodel' does not resolve to a ModelProviderConfig with a `model` field, and providers.models has no fallback entry. ``` These worked in the same runs: `/model ` with a matching `[[model_routes]]` entry (the next request asked for the route's model), and `zeroclaw agent -a main --model other-model -m hello` and the `model_switch` tool in a CLI turn (the next request asked for `other-model`). ### Expected behavior The reply to `/model ` and the `/model` status name the model the next request will use. If a profile's configured model is meant to stay pinned, the command should say so and name the model being served, not report a switch. `docs/book/src/providers/routing.md` says "`/model ` selects a model within the active provider profile." ### Steps to reproduce 1. Use a config with a provider profile that sets `model`, an agent on it, and a Telegram channel bound to that agent: ```toml [providers.models.custom.caller] uri = "http://127.0.0.1:18431/v1" model = "caller-model" [agents.main] channels = ["telegram.home"] model_provider = "custom.caller" ``` Add the usual `[channels.telegram.home]` block and a peer group that authorizes the sender, and bind `main` to existing risk and runtime profiles. Use a model id that is neither a route hint nor a route's model. 2. Run `zeroclaw channel start`. 3. Send `hello` and note the model the provider is asked for (`caller-model`). 4. Send `/model other-model`. The bot replies that the model was switched. 5. Send `hello`. The provider is asked for `caller-model` again. 6. Send `/model`. The status shows `other-model` as current. What ran was the real binary, Telegram channel and command handler. Two things were stood in: the Telegram Bot API, through `api_base_url`, by a local server that feeds updates and records `sendMessage` text; and the model provider, by a local OpenAI-compatible server that records the `model` field of each `/chat/completions` request. The replies quoted here are the recorded `sendMessage` text, which is why they carry `` tags. Only Telegram was run. The handler is shared by the channels in `supports_runtime_model_switch` (`crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs:2717`). ### Impact Someone who moves to a cheaper or stronger model with `/model ` keeps talking to, and paying for, the configured one, while the reply and the status both say otherwise. The workarounds are `/models .` to move to a profile pinned to the model you want, or a declared route whose target serves it. A route hint does not override a different pin on its target. ### Logs / stack traces Excerpt from the master run, with the status list shortened. The release reproduced the same mismatch. ```text user sends: 'hello one' request to provider: model='caller-model' bot reply (sendMessage): '[model=caller-model] ok' user sends: '/model other-model' bot reply (sendMessage): 'Model switched to other-model (model_provider: custom.caller). Context preserved.' user sends: 'hello two' request to provider: model='caller-model' bot reply (sendMessage): '[model=caller-model] ok' user sends: '/model' bot reply (sendMessage): 'Current model_provider: custom.caller\nCurrent model: other-model\nSwitch model with /model <model-id> or /model <hint>.\n\n...\n\nModel overrides (session-only; precedence user > agent > session > default):\n• user: —\n• agent: —\n• session (this chat): custom.caller / other-model\n• default (config): custom.caller / caller-model\n...' user sends: '/model third-model' bot reply (sendMessage): 'Model switched to third-model (model_provider: custom.caller). Context preserved.' user sends: 'hello three' request to provider: model='caller-model' bot reply (sendMessage): '[model=caller-model] ok' ``` Cause: the handler stores the id in the sender's route selection through `apply_model_ref` (`crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs:3283`) and builds its reply from that selection (`orchestrator/mod.rs:5492`). The channel's provider cache is keyed by provider profile, not by model (`provider_cache_key`, `orchestrator/mod.rs:4786`), and a profile with a configured model is built pinned (`new_pinned`, `crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/reliable.rs:1998`), which serves the pinned model whatever model is requested. I traced this by reading the code; #8693 reports the same mechanism. Related work: - #8693 is the same symptom in ZeroCode's `/model` picker. It was closed on 2026-07-08 through #8717, which applies live model switches to the provider. The channel path was not part of that fix. - #8600 tracks per-chat model selection. #9809 and the registry series starting at #12444 cover multi-model profiles, with channel binding changes in #12450. This report is about the success reply and the status on the current channel path. ### ZeroClaw version v0.9.0 (`6c78ba5`), and master `e02b7fb6f6` as a debug build (`zeroclaw 0.9.0 (v0.9.0-45-ge02b7fb6f6)`) ### Rust version rustc 1.96.1 ### Operating system macOS 26.5.2, arm64 ### Regression? Unknown ### Pre-flight checks - [X] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. - [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.body:
### Summary

The `browser` tool exposes 16 actions against an agent-browser backend that ships 100+ commands, leaving iframes, JS dialogs, tabs, and core form controls unreachable.

### Problem statement

`BrowserTool` resolves to one of three backends (`agent_browser` — the default per `default_browser_backend()` — `rust_native`, `computer_use`), but the action vocabulary is defined by a single `BrowserAction` enum with 16 variants (`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/browser.rs:135-197`):

`open`, `snapshot`, `click`, `fill`, `type`, `get_text`, `get_title`, `get_url`, `screenshot`, `wait`, `press`, `hover`, `scroll`, `is_visible`, `close`, `find`

plus six `computer_use`-only actions (`is_computer_use_only_action`, `browser.rs:2248-2253`): `mouse_move`, `mouse_click`, `mouse_drag`, `key_type`, `key_press`, `screen_capture`.

Checked against the installable backend (`agent-browser@0.34.0`, the version resolved by `npm install -g agent-browser` as documented in `docs/book/src/tools/browser.md`), the following command groups have no action mapping at all:

| Group | Backend commands with no ZeroClaw action | Consequence when the agent hits one |
|---|---|---|
| **Frames** | `frame <sel>`, `frame main` | Anything inside an iframe is unreachable. `snapshot` cannot enumerate it, `click`/`fill` cannot target it. Embedded checkout, OAuth, and captcha widgets are a hard wall, not a slow path. |
| **Dialogs** | `dialog accept [text]`, `dialog dismiss`, `dialog status` | `alert`/`beforeunload` are auto-accepted by the backend, but `confirm` and `prompt` require explicit handling. The page stays paused and every following action times out. |
| **Tabs / windows** | `tab`, `tab new [--label]`, `tab <id\|label>`, `tab close`, `window new`, `click --new-tab` | A `target=_blank` link or an OAuth popup opens a tab the tool cannot switch to. |
| **Form controls** | `select`, `check`, `uncheck`, `upload`, `dblclick`, `focus`, `drag`, `scrollintoview` | No dropdown selection, no checkbox toggle, no file upload. `find <...> check` reaches the backend's check action, but only via a located element — there is no standalone form-control action. |
| **Navigation** | `back`, `forward`, `reload`, `pushstate` | No history navigation of any kind. |
| **Reads** | `get html\|value\|attr\|count\|box\|styles`, `read` | Only `get text\|title\|url` are mapped. `read` in particular extracts agent-readable markdown **without launching Chrome** and supports `--outline`/`--filter`/`--llms`. |
| **Predicates** | `is enabled`, `is checked` | Only `is visible` is mapped (`browser.rs:694-697`). |
| **Diagnostics** | `console`, `errors`, `network requests\|route\|har`, `trace`, `profiler`, `highlight`, `diff snapshot\|screenshot` | The agent cannot read page console output or uncaught exceptions, so it cannot diagnose why its own action failed. |
| **Environment** | `set viewport\|device\|geo\|offline\|headers\|credentials\|media`, `cookies *`, `storage local\|session *` | No viewport control, no cookie or storage inspection. |
| **Other** | `eval`, `pdf`, `keyboard type\|inserttext`, `keydown`/`keyup`, `clipboard *`, `mouse move\|down\|up\|wheel`, `batch`, `state save\|load` | `eval` matters beyond its own utility: it is the generic escape hatch that would let an agent work around every row above. Without it the gaps have no workaround. |

Three narrower mismatches inside actions that *are* mapped:

1. **`find` cannot express the backend's full locator set.** The schema enum is `["role", "text", "label", "placeholder", "testid"]` (`browser.rs:1111-1114`); the backend also supports `alt`, `title`, `first`, `last`, and `nth`. The `--name` and `--exact` options are unreachable. Structurally, `nth` takes four positionals (`find nth <n> <sel> <action>`) which the current `find <by> <value> <action> [fill_value]` argument builder cannot produce (`browser.rs:699-716`).

2. **`wait` covers three of seven forms.** Mapped: selector, milliseconds, `--text`. Unmapped: `--url <glob>`, `--load <state>`, `--fn <js>`, `--state hidden`. `docs/book/src/tools/browser.md:248` shows `wait --load networkidle` as a manual CLI example, which is likely to read as an available tool capability.

3. **The backend's dialog `warning` is discarded.** When a JS dialog is pending, the backend sets a `warning` field on every command response. `AgentBrowserResponse` declares only `success`, `data`, and `error` (`browser.rs:114-119`) and `to_result` reads only `data` (`browser.rs:980-998`), so the field is dropped. This is what makes the dialog gap silent rather than diagnosable: the agent stalls with no signal about why.

Every action also costs one process spawn plus one daemon round-trip (`run_command`, `browser.rs:499-547`). The backend ships `batch` specifically to amortize that; a ten-step form flow currently pays ten spawns.

### Proposed solution

Extend `BrowserAction` in priority order, and make per-backend support explicit rather than implicit.

**Phase 1 — unblock stuck flows**
- `dialog` (`accept`/`dismiss`/`status`) and surface the backend `warning` field through `ToolResult` so a pending dialog is visible instead of manifesting as a timeout.
- `frame` (enter by selector / return to main).

**Phase 2 — form and navigation basics**
- `select`, `check`, `uncheck`, `upload`, `dblclick`, `focus`, `scrollintoview`.
- `back`, `forward`, `reload`.
- `is enabled`, `is checked`.

**Phase 3 — observability**
- `get html|value|attr|count`, `console`, `errors`.

**Phase 4 — behind explicit policy**
- `eval`, `cookies`, `storage`, `upload` path scoping, `set headers|credentials`. These read or inject page state and credentials; they should gate on `SecurityPolicy` rather than register alongside `get_title`. `eval` is a distinct category in the backend's own `--confirm-actions eval,download` grouping, and the current omission may well be a deliberate unstated choice — this issue asks for the decision to be recorded either way, not necessarily reversed.

**Phase 5 — throughput**
- Map multi-step sequences onto `batch`.

**Cross-backend capability matrix.** The three backends cannot cover the same set: WebDriver (`rust_native`, fantoccini) natively supports frame switching and `select` but has no console/network access; `computer_use` is coordinate-level only and supports none of the DOM actions. Each new variant needs a declared support set and a clear per-backend error, following the existing `unavailable_action_for_backend_error` pattern (`browser.rs:1177-1183`) rather than silently degrading.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- No change to whether the `browser` tool registers by default or is auto-approved — that surface belongs to #9824.
- No `eval` in the default action set. Phase 4 is a policy-gated proposal, not an unconditional expansion.
- No agent-browser version pinning or vendoring, and no change to the other two backends' availability probes.
- Not a fix for the unbounded subprocess wait in `run_command`; that is a separate defect filed alongside this issue.

### Alternatives considered

- **Status quo plus documentation.** Write the gaps down in `docs/book/src/tools/browser.md` so the model is not led to attempt unsupported flows. Cheap, but iframes and dialogs stay unreachable, and a stuck `confirm` dialog still burns a turn.
- **Expose `eval` only** and let the model synthesize the rest in JavaScript. Smallest diff and it does unblock every row, but it converts a bounded action vocabulary into arbitrary in-page code execution, and it cannot work on `rust_native` (no console) or `computer_use` at all.
- **Pass through arbitrary agent-browser argv.** Maximum coverage for minimum code, but it discards the allowlist and policy layer entirely and couples the tool contract to an upstream CLI's argument stability.
- **Drop the `agent_browser` backend and standardize on `rust_native`.** WebDriver covers frames and `select` natively, but loses `snapshot` ref quality, `read`, console/network access, and the documented default install path.

### Acceptance criteria

- An agent can complete a form inside an iframe: `frame` → `snapshot` → `fill` → `select` → `click` → `frame main`.
- A `confirm` dialog is resolvable via `dialog accept` and, while pending, is visible in the tool result rather than only as a downstream timeout.
- Each new action declares which of the three backends support it; unsupported combinations return the existing "not available for backend" style error, not a silent no-op.
- `docs/book/src/tools/browser.md` documents the supported action set per backend, and the parity table is derived from one source rather than restated per doc page.
- Tests cover action parsing and per-backend routing at the `parse_browser_action` / `execute_action` boundary.

### Architecture impact

`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/browser.rs` (the `BrowserAction` enum, `parse_browser_action`, `parameters_schema`, and all three backend dispatchers including the `native_backend` module), `crates/zeroclaw-config` only if Phase 4 introduces policy keys, and `docs/book/src/tools/browser.md`.

### Risk and rollback

Adding actions widens what a compromised or prompt-injected input can drive through a logged-in browser session. Phases 1-3 stay within the read/click/fill class already reachable today. Phase 4 does not, which is why it is proposed as policy-gated and separable. Each phase is an independent PR and revertible alone; reverting removes actions from `parameters_schema`, so no persisted state or config migration is involved.

### Expected routing

Needs design or RFC discussion first

### Next decision surface

#9824 (`type:tracker`, `status:in-progress`, milestone v0.9.0) is changing the default gating of this same tool — its PR 1 splits `[browser].enabled` and defaults automation off. The two are compatible (that issue changes the gate, this one changes the surface behind the gate), but the phase ordering and the Phase 4 policy question should be settled against it. Suggested sequencing: settle the capability matrix and Phase 1-2 scope after #9824 PR 1 lands, and route Phase 4 through the maintainer decision that #9824 is already establishing for browser automation defaults.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [X] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [X] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.title: [Bug]: Matrix tool-approval prompts are posted to the room timeline instead of the thread the turn runs in

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

issues.body:
### Affected component

channel

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

With `reply_in_thread = true`, each Matrix thread works as a separate conversation, and the bot's replies go into the thread. When a tool call in that turn needs approval, the approval prompt (`<TOKEN> approve/deny/always`) is sent to the room's main timeline, not the thread.

In a busy room, or with several threads waiting on approvals at once, the operator can't tell which conversation a prompt belongs to. The thread also shows no sign that it's blocked waiting for approval.

Cause: the approval path has nowhere to carry a thread.

- `ChannelApprovalRequest` (`crates/zeroclaw-api/src/channel.rs`) holds the tool name, arguments summary, raw arguments and batch position. It has no thread field.
- The approval gate (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/turn/approval_gate.rs`) passes only `ctx.channel_reply_target` as the recipient. The turn context has no thread field.
- Matrix keeps the thread separately from the recipient: `reply_target` is the bare room ID and the thread goes in `ChannelMessage::thread_ts`. Normal replies are threaded because the orchestrator calls `.in_thread(msg.thread_ts)`. `MatrixChannel::request_approval_attributed` builds `SendMessage::new(prompt, recipient)` without a thread, so the prompt goes to the room's main timeline.

Mattermost doesn't have this problem, because it puts the thread into the recipient string (`channel_id:root_id`) and the approval prompt reuses it.


### Expected behavior

The approval prompt is posted in the same thread as the turn that triggered it, just like the bot's normal replies. Replying in the thread already resolves the approval, because the token parser reads only the message text, so only where the prompt is sent needs to change.

## Possible fix

Carry the thread on the approval path: add an optional thread anchor to `ChannelApprovalRequest` (or `channel_thread` on the turn context next to `channel_reply_target`), fill it in from the incoming message's `thread_ts`, and have Matrix call `.in_thread(...)` when sending the prompt. This keeps `msg.thread_ts` as the single place the thread is stored, rather than packing the thread into Matrix's recipient string (Matrix uses the bare room ID as the recipient for room resolution, allowlists and draft keys). Other channels that keep the thread outside the recipient may have the same gap; I've only checked Matrix and Mattermost.


### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# 1. Configure a Matrix channel with threaded replies and a tool that needs approval:
#    [channels.matrix.<alias>]
#    reply_in_thread = true
#    (autonomy set so that e.g. `shell` requires approval)
# 2. In a room the bot is in, start a thread (or send a message the bot answers in a thread).
# 3. In that thread, ask the bot to do something that calls the approval-gated tool.
# 4. Observe: the approval prompt appears in the room's main timeline, not in the thread.
```

### Impact

Affected users: Matrix operators who use `reply_in_thread` and have approval-gated tools.
Frequency: always.
Consequence: approval prompts are separated from their conversation. With several threads waiting on approvals at once, the operator has to match prompts to threads by guesswork.


### Logs / stack traces

```text

```

### ZeroClaw version

3773cae2d

### Rust version

rustc 1.100.0

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

issues.title: [Feature]: Make Docker dependency caching reliable across CI builders and review stub prefetch
issues.body:
### Summary

Make Docker dependency caching reliable across fresh CI builders and prevent dummy workspace artifacts from leaking into production builds; evaluate completing the current approach versus cargo-chef or direct-source builds.

### Problem statement

The current source-image Dockerfiles combine hand-written workspace stubs, a dependency-prefetch build, BuildKit cache mounts, real-source restoration, and manual artifact invalidation. This needs a focused correctness and cache-effectiveness review.

Source inspected on master at `74c8af5cf66eadae7246e2ae437886578bd96734`:

- [Dockerfile: stub creation and prefetch](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/74c8af5cf66eadae7246e2ae437886578bd96734/Dockerfile#L123-L170), with equivalent flows in `Dockerfile.debian` and `Dockerfile.alpine`. The prefetch writes compiled dependencies into `/app/target` using `RUN --mount=type=cache`.
- [Dockerfile: real-source restoration and manual invalidation](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/74c8af5cf66eadae7246e2ae437886578bd96734/Dockerfile#L172-L224). The rules must account for workspace libraries, procedural macros, build scripts, and host/target output directories.
- [PR source-image workflow](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/74c8af5cf66eadae7246e2ae437886578bd96734/.github/workflows/docker-image-pr.yml#L187-L201) exports/imports `type=gha` layer caches, without a separate mechanism to persist the Cargo cache mounts.
- [Source-image publishing workflow](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/74c8af5cf66eadae7246e2ae437886578bd96734/.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml#L191-L213) has no explicit external build-cache configuration for this step.

Docker's [cache-mount documentation](https://docs.docker.com/build/ci/github-actions/cache/#cache-mounts) states: “BuildKit doesn't preserve cache mounts in the GitHub Actions cache by default.” Consequently, a cached prefetch instruction does not imply its `/app/target` contents are restored on a fresh builder. Persistent local builders can benefit, and unchanged whole-image layers can still be reused; the gap concerns compilation reuse after source changes on a new CI builder.

There is also a correctness symptom worth investigating: the [source-image build on #11634](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/45096246466/job/137436631859) reports these errors:

```text
error[E0432]: unresolved import `zeroclaw_api::lifecycle`
error[E0433]: cannot find `jsonrpc` in `zeroclaw_api`
```

These are observed build errors, not proof that stub reuse is their sole cause. The cache-persistence gap above is established from configuration and Docker's documented behavior; current-master build failures and before/after timings still need remote validation.

Related work checked before filing:

- #4729 proposed cargo-chef; closed without merging.
- #9980 tested a different cache backend; closed without merging after its author reported no consistent warm-build benefit and recommended restructuring dependency caching. Those historical measurements are not a benchmark of today's master.
- #5885 tracked workspace COPY fragility; closed. #7108 tracked broader Rust CI performance; closed.
- #11738 and #12212 repaired individual prefetch inputs; useful context, but not a solution to cache-mount persistence.

No open issue or PR specifically covering this combined Docker dependency-cache correctness and persistence gap was found in the searches for cargo-chef, Docker caching, cache mounts, and prefetch/stub handling.

### Proposed solution

Choose one approach based on GitHub CI evidence, rather than assuming that changing only the cache backend will help:

1. **Complete the existing approach.** Preserve prefetch, but either explicitly persist/restore Cargo cache mounts or store reusable dependency artifacts in exportable image layers. Make stub invalidation cover all relevant workspace artifacts, including host-side procedural macros/build scripts. Keep compiler, target, libc, profile, and feature variants appropriately separated, with safe fork-PR cache access.
2. **Replace hand-written prefetch with cargo-chef.** Generate a dependency recipe and let a pinned cargo-chef version manage the skeleton and dummy cleanup. Ensure cooked dependencies actually survive external cache export; merely adding cargo-chef while leaving all artifacts in unpersisted mounts would retain the persistence gap. Validate the default GNU cross-build and Alpine cargo-zigbuild paths.
3. **Remove prefetch and build real sources directly.** Keep Cargo registry/git/target cache mounts and explicitly arrange persistence when cross-runner reuse is required. This removes dummy artifacts and manual invalidation, with a potential cold-build cost that should be measured.

### Non-goals / out of scope

No Rust/MSRV/version bumps, application changes, release-profile reductions, weaker smoke tests, runner-provider migration, or nextest installer changes. No need to adopt every alternative or make a repository-wide build-system decision before a bounded fix.

### Alternatives considered

- Adding one more crate-specific COPY/cleanup exception may unblock a build, but does not address cache persistence or the maintenance burden.
- Changing only the remote cache backend has already been explored in #9980 and should not be repeated without evidence that the dependency artifacts are being saved and restored.
- Keeping the current behavior leaves correctness dependent on hand-maintained rules and cross-runner dependency reuse unproven.

### Acceptance criteria

- Run validation on GitHub CI: cold build, same-revision rebuild, source-only change, and dependency/lockfile change, each on a fresh builder where applicable.
- Report restored layers/artifacts, actual Cargo compilation activity, elapsed time, and cache transfer/storage cost; distinguish warm-builder from fresh-builder results.
- Verify default amd64/arm64, Debian amd64, Alpine amd64/arm64, and the existing additional feature lanes; preserve runtime smoke checks and real-binary checks.
- Confirm that no dummy workspace binary/library/build-script artifact is used in the final build and investigate the linked missing-module failure independently.
- Document what is cached, where it lives, how variants are isolated, which events may write it, and how it is invalidated. Cover both PR validation and publishing, or explicitly document a deliberate difference.

### Architecture impact

Source Dockerfiles, Docker PR/publishing workflows, existing container architecture guards, and CI documentation. Runtime behavior and container interfaces should remain unchanged. Ordinary tooling/CI triage is sufficient unless maintainers identify a broader decision.

### Risk and rollback

Risks include reusing incompatible artifacts, excessive cache size/transfer cost, cross-compilation regressions, and unsafe cache writes from untrusted PRs. Preserve existing trust boundaries and use immutable tool/action pins. Revert the implementation commit and use a new cache namespace or invalidate the affected cache if necessary; builds must remain correct with an empty cache.

### Expected routing

Ordinary feature triage

### Next decision surface

Maintainer triage on this issue: select a bounded approach and use a focused PR with remote before/after measurements. Reference #4729 and #9980 when assessing previous attempts.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [X] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [X] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

prs.title: feat(config): introduce independent provider registry domain types
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (stacked review; merge after #12448)
- **What changed and why:** Introduce the typed provider registry domain for connections, capabilities, model references, presets, overrides, and fallback validation. Add the model/API resolution primitives that later layers consume.
- **Scope boundary:** This layer owns registry domain types and validation/resolution only. Runtime activation, registry editing RPCs, provider construction, CLI, ZeroCode, and Web consumers remain in later stacked PRs.
- **Blast radius:** `zeroclaw-api` capability contracts and `zeroclaw-config` provider-registry types/resolution. No active user-facing consumer is switched in this layer.
- **Linked issue(s):** Depends on #12448. Related to #12450. This stacked series supersedes #9809 (closed).

### What this does, simply

A connection describes how to reach a provider, while a model entry describes a concrete model and capability exposed through that connection. This layer gives those concepts typed representations and a single resolver for inherited API options, explicit `null` clearing, model-level wire API selection, capability validation, and provider fallback graph validation. Later layers can build consumers on this canonical boundary without duplicating TOML parsing or provider/model lookup.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

The incremental diff is limited to the provider registry domain and its API/config resolution surface.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A; no CLI, web, TUI, or channel surface changes.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `8ae63adb4e`; full behavior validation is provided by the GitHub CI checks on this exact head.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** Registry construction now has one typed source for connection/model/capability resolution, including ASR timeout inheritance, explicit timeout clearing, complete endpoint overrides, and per-kind wire API validation without requiring a connection defaults table. Resolver regressions also cover fallback duplicate/cycle rejection. Secret masking/restoration failures are returned to export, gateway, and RPC callers instead of being silently discarded.

- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
